Random variables and discrete random variables

A random variable turns outcomes into numbers; for a discrete one, everything (probabilities of events, the CDF, the mean, the variance) comes from its PMF. In past papers this topic lives in Quiz 1: almost every year it asks for a derivation from the definition (mean and variance of the Geometric, Binomial or Poisson; E[X]=∑P(X>i)E[X]=\sum P(X\gt i)E[X]=∑P(X>i); P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a)P(a\lt X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a); Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X)) plus a definitions question (random variable, Borel σ-algebra, PPP, PXP_XPX​, FXF_XFX​, memorylessness). The end-sems of 2023–25 never asked a named discrete distribution on its own, but every later topic uses these tools, so the derivations must be fluent. This bank has every past-paper question of the topic, every 2026 and 2025 tutorial and homework question on it, and derivation-style extras from ProbabilityCourse and Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, each with a full solution written the way the course keys grade. A printable question list (PDF) has the same questions with tick boxes.

2. Expectation, variance and functions of a discrete RV: Q1-22.4, Q1-22.5, Q1-24.1, Q1-26.2

3. Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson: Q1-25.2, MS23.B2b, Q1-23.6

4. Geometric distribution and memorylessness: Q1-24.2

What is inside

    1  Random variables, PMF and CDF · Lectures 4–5

    Theory recap

    A random variable replaces a complicated sample space by numbers. Every probability about XXX is computed by pulling the question back to Ω\OmegaΩ: PX(B)=P(X−1(B))P_X(B)=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B)=P(X−1(B)). The PMF and the CDF are this one rule applied to points and to half-lines.

    Definition: random variable

    A random variable is a map X:(Ω,F,P)→(R,B(R),PX)X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R),P_X)X:(Ω,F,P)→(R,B(R),PX​) such that for every Borel set B∈B(R)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B∈B(R) the inverse image X−1(B):={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}∈F.X^{-1}(B):=\{\omega\in\Omega: X(\omega)\in B\}\in\mathcal F .X−1(B):={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}∈F. This "(F,B)(\mathcal F,\mathcal B)(F,B)-measurability" is exactly what makes P(X−1(B))\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))P(X−1(B)) defined. If the range Ω′\Omega'Ω′ of XXX is countable, XXX is a discrete random variable (then one may take F′=\mathcal F'=F′= power set of Ω′\Omega'Ω′).

    Definition: Borel σ-algebra

    B(R)\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B(R) is the smallest σ-algebra on R\mathbb RR containing all open intervals (a,b)(a,b)(a,b). It also contains [a,b][a,b][a,b], [a,b)[a,b)[a,b), (a,∞)(a,\infty)(a,∞), [a,∞)[a,\infty)[a,∞), (−∞,b](-\infty,b](−∞,b], (−∞,b)(-\infty,b)(−∞,b) and single points {a}\{a\}{a} (each is a countable union/intersection/complement of open intervals, e.g. {a}=⋂n(a−1n,a+1n)\{a\}=\bigcap_n(a-\tfrac1n,a+\tfrac1n){a}=⋂n​(a−n1​,a+n1​)).

    P, P_X, p_X and F_X
    • P\mathbb PP: the probability measure on (Ω,F)(\Omega,\mathcal F)(Ω,F).
    • Induced measure: PX(B):=P(X−1(B))P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B):=P(X−1(B)), B∈B(R)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B∈B(R). It is a probability measure on (R,B(R))(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))(R,B(R)).
    • PMF (discrete XXX): pX(x):=PX({x})=P({ω:X(ω)=x})p_X(x):=P_X(\{x\})=\mathbb P(\{\omega:X(\omega)=x\})pX​(x):=PX​({x})=P({ω:X(ω)=x}).
    • CDF: FX(x):=PX((−∞,x])=P({ω:X(ω)≤x})=∑u≤xpX(u)F_X(x):=P_X((-\infty,x])=\mathbb P(\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\})=\sum_{u\le x}p_X(u)FX​(x):=PX​((−∞,x])=P({ω:X(ω)≤x})=∑u≤x​pX​(u).
    • Back again: PX(B)=∑x∈BpX(x)P_X(B)=\sum_{x\in B}p_X(x)PX​(B)=∑x∈B​pX​(x), and pX(x)=FX(x)−FX(x−)p_X(x)=F_X(x)-F_X(x^-)pX​(x)=FX​(x)−FX​(x−) (the jump at xxx).
    A legitimate PMF

    pX(x)≥0p_X(x)\ge 0pX​(x)≥0 and ∑x∈Ω′pX(x)=1\sum_{x\in\Omega'}p_X(x)=1∑x∈Ω′​pX​(x)=1. Proof of the second: the events {X=x}\{X=x\}{X=x}, x∈Ω′x\in\Omega'x∈Ω′, are disjoint with union Ω\OmegaΩ, so by countable additivity ∑xpX(x)=P(⋃x{X=x})=P(Ω)=1\sum_x p_X(x)=\mathbb P\big(\bigcup_x\{X=x\}\big)=\mathbb P(\Omega)=1∑x​pX​(x)=P(⋃x​{X=x})=P(Ω)=1.

    Unknown constants in a PMF: impose both conditions. Normalisation gives one equation; non-negativity of every mass gives the allowed range.

    CDF properties
    • FXF_XFX​ is non-decreasing, right-continuous, FX(−∞)=0F_X(-\infty)=0FX​(−∞)=0, FX(∞)=1F_X(\infty)=1FX​(∞)=1.
    • For a discrete XXX it is a staircase: flat between support points, jump of size pX(x)p_X(x)pX​(x) at each support point, closed dot on the upper step.
    • P(a<X≤b)=FX(b)−FX(a)\mathbb P(a\lt X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)P(a<X≤b)=FX​(b)−FX​(a) for a<ba\lt ba<b (proof: {X≤b}={X≤a}∪{a<X≤b}\{X\le b\}=\{X\le a\}\cup\{a\lt X\le b\}{X≤b}={X≤a}∪{a<X≤b}, disjoint, then the additivity axiom).
    • P(X>x)=1−FX(x)\mathbb P(X\gt x)=1-F_X(x)P(X>x)=1−FX​(x); P(X≥x)=1−FX(x)+pX(x)\mathbb P(X\ge x)=1-F_X(x)+p_X(x)P(X≥x)=1−FX​(x)+pX​(x).
    Watch out

    P(a≤X≤b)\mathbb P(a\le X\le b)P(a≤X≤b), P(a<X<b)\mathbb P(a\lt X\lt b)P(a<X<b) and P(a<X≤b)\mathbb P(a\lt X\le b)P(a<X≤b) differ for a discrete XXX by the masses at aaa and bbb. Only the half-open interval (a,b](a,b](a,b] gives F(b)−F(a)F(b)-F(a)F(b)−F(a) exactly.

    Q1-25.3Define a random variable and the Borel σ-algebra; relate P, P_X and F_X 2025 Quiz 1 · Q3 · 10 marks★ Must-do

    Define the following: 1) A random variable 2) Borel sigma algebra. For a random variable XXX describe all possible relationships between P\mathbb{P}P, PXP_XPX​ and FX(⋅)F_X(\cdot)FX​(⋅).

    Solution · follows the official key

    1) Random variable

    Let (Ω,F,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)(Ω,F,P) be a probability space. A random variable is a function X:Ω→RX:\Omega\to\mathbb RX:Ω→R that is (F,B(R))(\mathcal F,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))(F,B(R))-measurable: for every Borel set B∈B(R)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B∈B(R), X−1(B)={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}∈F.X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega\in\Omega: X(\omega)\in B\}\in\mathcal F.X−1(B)={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}∈F. (Picture: a set BBB on the real line is pulled back by X−1X^{-1}X−1 to a set of sample points inside Ω\OmegaΩ; measurability says this pre-image is an event, so P\mathbb PP can measure it.)

    2) Borel σ-algebra

    B(R)\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B(R) is the smallest σ-algebra on R\mathbb RR that contains every open interval (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), a<ba\lt ba<b. Equivalently it is generated by intervals of any one kind, e.g. all (−∞,x](-\infty,x](−∞,x]. It contains all closed and half-open intervals and all singletons, e.g. (−∞,x]=⋂n(−∞,x+1n)(-\infty,x]=\bigcap_{n}(-\infty,x+\tfrac1n)(−∞,x]=⋂n​(−∞,x+n1​) and {a}=⋂n(a−1n,a+1n)\{a\}=\bigcap_n (a-\tfrac1n,a+\tfrac1n){a}=⋂n​(a−n1​,a+n1​).

    3) Relations between P\mathbb PP, PXP_XPX​, FXF_XFX​

    • P\mathbb PP is the measure on (Ω,F)(\Omega,\mathcal F)(Ω,F).
    • XXX induces a probability measure on (R,B(R))(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))(R,B(R)): PX(B):=P(X−1(B))P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B):=P(X−1(B)). It satisfies the axioms because X−1X^{-1}X−1 preserves complements and countable disjoint unions.
    • The CDF is PXP_XPX​ on half-lines: FX(x)=PX((−∞,x])=P({ω:X(ω)≤x})F_X(x)=P_X((-\infty,x])=\mathbb P(\{\omega: X(\omega)\le x\})FX​(x)=PX​((−∞,x])=P({ω:X(ω)≤x}).
    • Conversely FXF_XFX​ determines PXP_XPX​: PX((a,b])=FX(b)−FX(a)P_X((a,b])=F_X(b)-F_X(a)PX​((a,b])=FX​(b)−FX​(a), and the half-open intervals generate B(R)\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B(R).
    • Discrete XXX: pX(x)=PX({x})p_X(x)=P_X(\{x\})pX​(x)=PX​({x}), FX(x)=∑u≤xpX(u)F_X(x)=\sum_{u\le x}p_X(u)FX​(x)=∑u≤x​pX​(u), PX(B)=∑x∈BpX(x)P_X(B)=\sum_{x\in B}p_X(x)PX​(B)=∑x∈B​pX​(x).
    • Continuous XXX: FX(x)=∫−∞xfX(t) dtF_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t)\,dtFX​(x)=∫−∞x​fX​(t)dt, PX(B)=∫BfX(t) dtP_X(B)=\int_B f_X(t)\,dtPX​(B)=∫B​fX​(t)dt, fX=FX′f_X=F_X'fX​=FX′​.
    Answer

    XXX is measurable: X−1(B)∈F ∀B∈B(R)X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F\ \forall B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)X−1(B)∈F ∀B∈B(R); B(R)=σ(open intervals)\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\sigma(\text{open intervals})B(R)=σ(open intervals); PX(B)=P(X−1(B))P_X(B)=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B)=P(X−1(B)), FX(x)=PX((−∞,x])=P(X≤x)F_X(x)=P_X((-\infty,x])=\mathbb P(X\le x)FX​(x)=PX​((−∞,x])=P(X≤x), and FXF_XFX​ determines PXP_XPX​.

    What the grader checks
    • Measurability condition X−1(B)∈FX^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal FX−1(B)∈F stated (not just "a function from Ω to ℝ").
    • Borel σ-algebra as the σ-algebra generated by open intervals.
    • The chain P→PX→FX\mathbb P\to P_X\to F_XP→PX​→FX​ with formulas, plus the PMF/PDF special cases. (No marks split shown in the key.)
    Q1-26.4acdConcept check: random variable; P, P_X, p_X, F_X; memorylessness 2026 Quiz 1 · Q4 (items 1, 3, 4)★ Must-do

    Concept-check: Give definitions/explanations for the following: 1. Random variable 3. Discrete random variable: relations between PPP, PXP_XPX​, pX(⋅)p_X(\cdot)pX​(⋅) and FX(⋅)F_X(\cdot)FX​(⋅) 4. Memoryless property of Geometric or exponential random variable.

    (Item 2, σ-algebra, belongs to topic 1.)

    Solution · follows the official key

    1. Random variable

    A random variable XXX is a map X:(Ω,F,P)→(R,B(R),PX)X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R),P_X)X:(Ω,F,P)→(R,B(R),PX​) such that for each B∈B(R)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B∈B(R) the inverse image X−1(B):={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}X^{-1}(B):=\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}X−1(B):={ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B} satisfies X−1(B)∈FX^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal FX−1(B)∈F and PX(B)=P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B})P_X(B)=P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\})PX​(B)=P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}).

    3. Discrete random variable: PPP, PXP_XPX​, pXp_XpX​, FXF_XFX​

    • Original measure PPP on (Ω,F)(\Omega,\mathcal F)(Ω,F): assigns probabilities to events about sample points.
    • Induced measure PX(B):=P(X−1(B))P_X(B):=P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B):=P(X−1(B)), B∈B(R)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)B∈B(R).
    • PMF pX(x):=P(X=x)=PX({x})p_X(x):=P(X=x)=P_X(\{x\})pX​(x):=P(X=x)=PX​({x}).
    • CDF FX(x):=P({ω:X(ω)≤x})=PX((−∞,x])=∑u≤xpX(u)F_X(x):=P(\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\})=P_X((-\infty,x])=\sum_{u\le x}p_X(u)FX​(x):=P({ω:X(ω)≤x})=PX​((−∞,x])=∑u≤x​pX​(u).

    4. Memoryless property

    XXX is memoryless if P(X>s+t∣X>s)=P(X>t)P(X\gt s+t\mid X\gt s)=P(X\gt t)P(X>s+t∣X>s)=P(X>t) for all s,t≥0s,t\ge0s,t≥0 (integers for a geometric).

    Geometric. pN(k)=(1−p)k−1pp_N(k)=(1-p)^{k-1}ppN​(k)=(1−p)k−1p, k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dotsk=1,2,… Then P(N>k)=∑j>k(1−p)j−1p=(1−p)kP(N\gt k)=\sum_{j\gt k}(1-p)^{j-1}p=(1-p)^kP(N>k)=∑j>k​(1−p)j−1p=(1−p)k (the first kkk trials all fail). For k,m≥0k,m\ge0k,m≥0, since {N>k+m}⊆{N>k}\{N\gt k+m\}\subseteq\{N\gt k\}{N>k+m}⊆{N>k}, P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k+m)P(N>k)=(1−p)k+m(1−p)k=(1−p)m=P(N>m).P(N\gt k+m\mid N\gt k)=\frac{P(N\gt k+m)}{P(N\gt k)}=\frac{(1-p)^{k+m}}{(1-p)^k}=(1-p)^m=P(N\gt m).P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k)P(N>k+m)​=(1−p)k(1−p)k+m​=(1−p)m=P(N>m).

    Or exponential. P(X>x)=e−λxP(X\gt x)=e^{-\lambda x}P(X>x)=e−λx, so P(X>s+t∣X>s)=e−λ(s+t)/e−λs=e−λt=P(X>t)P(X\gt s+t\mid X\gt s)=e^{-\lambda(s+t)}/e^{-\lambda s}=e^{-\lambda t}=P(X\gt t)P(X>s+t∣X>s)=e−λ(s+t)/e−λs=e−λt=P(X>t).

    Answer

    Definitions as above; P(N>k+m∣N>k)=(1−p)m=P(N>m)P(N\gt k+m\mid N\gt k)=(1-p)^m=P(N\gt m)P(N>k+m∣N>k)=(1−p)m=P(N>m) (geometric) or e−λte^{-\lambda t}e−λt (exponential).

    What the grader checks
    • The map with domain and codomain triples, the measurability condition and PX(B)=P(X−1(B))P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))PX​(B)=P(X−1(B)).
    • All four objects with their formulas, including FX=∑u≤xpX(u)F_X=\sum_{u\le x}p_X(u)FX​=∑u≤x​pX​(u).
    • Memorylessness: the statement, the tail P(N>k)=(1−p)kP(N\gt k)=(1-p)^kP(N>k)=(1−p)k, the ratio of tails.
    Q1-23.1Prove P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a) 2023 Quiz 1 · Q1 · 5 marks2022 Quiz 1 · Q1 · 5 marks★ Must-do

    Consider a discrete random variable XXX. Prove that for a,b∈Ra,b\in\mathbb{R}a,b∈R and a<ba\lt ba<b, P(a<X≤b)=FX(b)−FX(a)P(a\lt X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)P(a<X≤b)=FX​(b)−FX​(a) where FX(⋅)F_X(\cdot)FX​(⋅) denotes the CDF of XXX.

    Same as Q1-22.1 (2022 Quiz 1 Q1, which also gives the definition FX(x)=P(ω:X(ω)≤x)=∑x1≤xpX(x1)F_X(x)=\mathbb P(\omega: X(\omega)\le x)=\sum_{x_1\le x}p_X(x_1)FX​(x)=P(ω:X(ω)≤x)=∑x1​≤x​pX​(x1​)). Do it once.

    Solution · follows the official key

    CDF. FX(x)=P(X≤x)=P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)≤x})=∑u≤xpX(u)F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\le x\})=\sum_{u\le x}p_X(u)FX​(x)=P(X≤x)=P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)≤x})=∑u≤x​pX​(u).

    Events. For a<ba\lt ba<b define C={X≤a},D={a<X≤b},E={X≤b}.C=\{X\le a\},\qquad D=\{a\lt X\le b\},\qquad E=\{X\le b\}.C={X≤a},D={a<X≤b},E={X≤b}. Each is the inverse image of a Borel set ((−∞,a](-\infty,a](−∞,a], (a,b](a,b](a,b], (−∞,b](-\infty,b](−∞,b]), so each is an event.

    Disjoint union. C∩D=∅C\cap D=\varnothingC∩D=∅ (no ω\omegaω has X(ω)≤aX(\omega)\le aX(ω)≤a and X(ω)>aX(\omega)\gt aX(ω)>a), and C∪D=EC\cup D=EC∪D=E because a<ba\lt ba<b: if X(ω)≤bX(\omega)\le bX(ω)≤b then either X(ω)≤aX(\omega)\le aX(ω)≤a or a<X(ω)≤ba\lt X(\omega)\le ba<X(ω)≤b.

    Axiom 3 (additivity) for disjoint events: P(E)=P(C)+P(D) ⟹ P(X≤b)=P(X≤a)+P(a<X≤b).P(E)=P(C)+P(D)\ \Longrightarrow\ P(X\le b)=P(X\le a)+P(a\lt X\le b).P(E)=P(C)+P(D) ⟹ P(X≤b)=P(X≤a)+P(a<X≤b). Rearranging,

    Answer

    P(a<X≤b)=P(X≤b)−P(X≤a)=FX(b)−FX(a).P(a\lt X\le b)=P(X\le b)-P(X\le a)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).P(a<X≤b)=P(X≤b)−P(X≤a)=FX​(b)−FX​(a).

    What the grader checks (2023 key)
    • 1 mark: CDF definition.
    • 2 marks: writing the disjoint sets CCC, DDD with C∪D=EC\cup D=EC∪D=E and invoking the third axiom.
    • 2 marks: the logic (why they are disjoint, why the union is EEE, the rearrangement).
    RQ22.A5aNormalising constant of p(x) = C·2^(−x) 2022 Replacement Quiz · Sec. 1 Q5 part 1 · 2 marks★ Must-do

    Let XXX and YYY be independent and identically distributed discrete random variables taking values on positive integers. Their pmf is p(x)=C2−xp(x) = C2^{-x}p(x)=C2−x for x≥1x \ge 1x≥1. Find the value of CCC that makes it a valid pmf.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Non-negativity needs C≥0C\ge0C≥0. Normalisation: the masses must sum to 1 over the support {1,2,… }\{1,2,\dots\}{1,2,…}. This is a geometric series with ratio 12<1\tfrac12\lt121​<1: ∑x=1∞C2−x=C⋅1/21−1/2=C=1.\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}C2^{-x}=C\cdot\frac{1/2}{1-1/2}=C=1.x=1∑∞​C2−x=C⋅1−1/21/2​=C=1.

    Answer

    C=1C=1C=1, i.e. p(x)=2−xp(x)=2^{-x}p(x)=2−x, x=1,2,…x=1,2,\dotsx=1,2,… (a Geometric(12)(\tfrac12)(21​) PMF).

    What the grader checks
    • Sum over the full support set equal to 1; geometric series summed correctly (2 marks).
    RQ22.A5cP(X divides Y) for i.i.d. p(x) = 2^(−x) 2022 Replacement Quiz · Sec. 1 Q5 part 3 · 2 marks★ Must-do

    (Same X,YX, YX,Y as in RQ22.A5a: i.i.d. on the positive integers with p(x)=2−xp(x)=2^{-x}p(x)=2−x.) Find P(X divides Y)P(X \text{ divides } Y)P(X divides Y).

    Solution · follows the official key

    Decompose the event. XXX divides YYY iff X=nX=nX=n and Y=knY=knY=kn for some integers n≥1n\ge1n≥1, k≥1k\ge1k≥1. These events are disjoint for different (n,k)(n,k)(n,k), so by countable additivity and independence, P(X∣Y)=∑n=1∞∑k=1∞P(X=n)P(Y=kn)=∑n=1∞2−n∑k=1∞2−kn.P(X\mid Y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(X=n)P(Y=kn)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-kn}.P(X∣Y)=n=1∑∞​k=1∑∞​P(X=n)P(Y=kn)=n=1∑∞​2−nk=1∑∞​2−kn.

    Inner geometric series (ratio 2−n<12^{-n}\lt12−n<1): ∑k≥1(2−n)k=2−n1−2−n=12n−1\sum_{k\ge1}(2^{-n})^k=\dfrac{2^{-n}}{1-2^{-n}}=\dfrac{1}{2^n-1}∑k≥1​(2−n)k=1−2−n2−n​=2n−11​. Hence P(X∣Y)=∑n=1∞12n(2n−1).P(X\mid Y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n(2^n-1)}.P(X∣Y)=n=1∑∞​2n(2n−1)1​.

    Partial fractions: 12n(2n−1)=12n−1−12n\dfrac{1}{2^n(2^n-1)}=\dfrac{1}{2^n-1}-\dfrac{1}{2^n}2n(2n−1)1​=2n−11​−2n1​, so the sum is ∑n≥112n−1−∑n≥12−n=∑n≥112n−1−1\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{2^n-1}-\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{2^n-1}-1∑n≥1​2n−11​−∑n≥1​2−n=∑n≥1​2n−11​−1. The series has no closed form; numerically it is 0.60670.60670.6067 (first terms 12+112+156+1240+…\tfrac12+\tfrac1{12}+\tfrac1{56}+\tfrac1{240}+\dots21​+121​+561​+2401​+…).

    Answer

    P(X divides Y)=∑n≥112n(2n−1)=∑n≥112n−1−1≈0.607.P(X\text{ divides }Y)=\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{2^n(2^n-1)}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{2^n-1}-1\approx0.607.P(X divides Y)=n≥1∑​2n(2n−1)1​=n≥1∑​2n−11​−1≈0.607.

    About the key

    The key's last line is garbled; it leaves the answer as a series. The value above was checked numerically (the sum converges fast: 20 terms give 0.606695).

    Q1-22.3PMF of winnings from two cards (hearts +2, spades −1) 2022 Quiz 1 · Q3 · 5 marks★ Must-do

    Two cards are chosen from a standard deck of 52 cards. Suppose that you win 2 Rs for each heart selected, and lose 1 Rs for each spade selected. Other suits (clubs or diamonds) bring neither win nor loss. Let XXX denote your winnings. Determine the probability mass function pX(x)p_X(x)pX​(x).

    Solution · follows the official key

    Range. Each card is H (+2, 13 cards), S (−1, 13 cards) or O = club/diamond (0, 26 cards). The pairs give HH→4,  HO→2,  HS→1,  OO→0,  SO→−1,  SS→−2,\text{HH}\to4,\ \ \text{HO}\to2,\ \ \text{HS}\to1,\ \ \text{OO}\to0,\ \ \text{SO}\to-1,\ \ \text{SS}\to-2,HH→4,  HO→2,  HS→1,  OO→0,  SO→−1,  SS→−2, so Ω′={−2,−1,0,1,2,4}\Omega'=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,4\}Ω′={−2,−1,0,1,2,4} (3 and values outside [−2,4][-2,4][−2,4] are impossible).

    Without replacement (the usual reading of "two cards are chosen"). Multiply along the draw order; a mixed pair can come in two orders, so it is doubled:

    • pX(4)=1352⋅1251=117p_X(4)=\frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{12}{51}=\frac1{17}pX​(4)=5213​⋅5112​=171​,  pX(−2)=1352⋅1251=117\ p_X(-2)=\frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{12}{51}=\frac1{17} pX​(−2)=5213​⋅5112​=171​
    • pX(2)=2⋅1352⋅2651=1351p_X(2)=2\cdot\frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{26}{51}=\frac{13}{51}pX​(2)=2⋅5213​⋅5126​=5113​,  pX(−1)=2⋅1352⋅2651=1351\ p_X(-1)=2\cdot\frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{26}{51}=\frac{13}{51} pX​(−1)=2⋅5213​⋅5126​=5113​
    • pX(1)=2⋅1352⋅1351=13102p_X(1)=2\cdot\frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{13}{51}=\frac{13}{102}pX​(1)=2⋅5213​⋅5113​=10213​,  pX(0)=2652⋅2551=25102\ p_X(0)=\frac{26}{52}\cdot\frac{25}{51}=\frac{25}{102} pX​(0)=5226​⋅5125​=10225​

    Check: 6+26+13+25+26+6102=1\frac{6+26+13+25+26+6}{102}=11026+26+13+25+26+6​=1.

    With replacement (the key also gives this, since the question does not say): each card independently H, S, O with probabilities 14,14,12\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac1241​,41​,21​: pX(4)=116p_X(4)=\tfrac1{16}pX​(4)=161​, pX(2)=2⋅14⋅12=14p_X(2)=2\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14pX​(2)=2⋅41​⋅21​=41​, pX(1)=2⋅116=18p_X(1)=2\cdot\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac18pX​(1)=2⋅161​=81​, pX(0)=14p_X(0)=\tfrac14pX​(0)=41​, pX(−1)=14p_X(-1)=\tfrac14pX​(−1)=41​, pX(−2)=116p_X(-2)=\tfrac1{16}pX​(−2)=161​.

    Answer
    xxx−2−10124
    without repl.1/1713/5125/10213/10213/511/17
    with repl.1/161/41/41/81/41/16

    pX(x)=0p_X(x)=0pX​(x)=0 for every other xxx.

    H25-03.7PMF and tails from the CDF 1 − (⌊x⌋+2)^(−s); tail-sum formula 2025 HW 3 Q7

    Let s>0s>0s>0 be a real parameter and let XXX be a non-negative integer valued random variable whose CDF is F(x)=0F(x)=0F(x)=0 for x<0x\lt0x<0 and F(x)=1−(⌊x⌋+2)−sF(x)=1-(\lfloor x\rfloor+2)^{-s}F(x)=1−(⌊x⌋+2)−s for x≥0x\ge0x≥0. Equivalently, for integer n≥0n\ge0n≥0, F(n)=1−(n+2)−sF(n)=1-(n+2)^{-s}F(n)=1−(n+2)−s.

    1. Show that the PMF of XXX is P(X=n)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s\mathbb{P}(X=n)=(n+1)^{-s}-(n+2)^{-s}P(X=n)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s, n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\dotsn=0,1,2,…, and verify that the probabilities sum to 1.
    2. (i) Show that P(X≥k)=(k+1)−s\mathbb{P}(X\ge k)=(k+1)^{-s}P(X≥k)=(k+1)−s, k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\dotsk=0,1,2,… (ii) Deduce P(X>k)=(k+2)−s\mathbb{P}(X>k)=(k+2)^{-s}P(X>k)=(k+2)−s.
    3. Prove that for any nonnegative integer-valued random variable XXX, E(X)=∑k=0∞P(X>k)\mathbb{E}(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(X>k)E(X)=∑k=0∞​P(X>k).
    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    (a)

    For an integer-valued XXX, the mass at nnn is the jump of the CDF: P(X=n)=F(n)−F(n−1)P(X=n)=F(n)-F(n-1)P(X=n)=F(n)−F(n−1). For n≥1n\ge1n≥1: (1−(n+2)−s)−(1−(n+1)−s)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s\big(1-(n+2)^{-s}\big)-\big(1-(n+1)^{-s}\big)=(n+1)^{-s}-(n+2)^{-s}(1−(n+2)−s)−(1−(n+1)−s)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s. For n=0n=0n=0: F(0)−F(−1)=1−2−s−0=1−s−2−sF(0)-F(-1)=1-2^{-s}-0=1^{-s}-2^{-s}F(0)−F(−1)=1−2−s−0=1−s−2−s, the same formula. Each mass is positive since t↦t−st\mapsto t^{-s}t↦t−s is decreasing.

    Sum (telescoping): ∑n=0N[(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s]=1−(N+2)−s→1\sum_{n=0}^{N}\big[(n+1)^{-s}-(n+2)^{-s}\big]=1-(N+2)^{-s}\to1∑n=0N​[(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s]=1−(N+2)−s→1 as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞ because s>0s\gt0s>0.

    (b)

    (i) P(X≥k)=1−P(X≤k−1)=1−F(k−1)=(k+1)−sP(X\ge k)=1-P(X\le k-1)=1-F(k-1)=(k+1)^{-s}P(X≥k)=1−P(X≤k−1)=1−F(k−1)=(k+1)−s for k≥1k\ge1k≥1; for k=0k=0k=0, P(X≥0)=1=1−sP(X\ge0)=1=1^{-s}P(X≥0)=1=1−s. (Or telescope ∑n≥k\sum_{n\ge k}∑n≥k​.) (ii) P(X>k)=P(X≥k+1)=(k+2)−sP(X\gt k)=P(X\ge k+1)=(k+2)^{-s}P(X>k)=P(X≥k+1)=(k+2)−s.

    (c)

    Write n=∑k=0n−11n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}1n=∑k=0n−1​1 and swap the order of summation (all terms are non-negative, so this is allowed): E[X]=∑n=0∞n P(X=n)=∑n=1∞∑k=0n−1P(X=n)=∑k=0∞∑n=k+1∞P(X=n)=∑k=0∞P(X>k).E[X]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\,P(X=n)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}P(X=n)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=k+1}^{\infty}P(X=n)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P(X\gt k).E[X]=n=0∑∞​nP(X=n)=n=1∑∞​k=0∑n−1​P(X=n)=k=0∑∞​n=k+1∑∞​P(X=n)=k=0∑∞​P(X>k).

    Answer

    P(X=n)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−sP(X=n)=(n+1)^{-s}-(n+2)^{-s}P(X=n)=(n+1)−s−(n+2)−s, P(X≥k)=(k+1)−sP(X\ge k)=(k+1)^{-s}P(X≥k)=(k+1)−s, P(X>k)=(k+2)−sP(X\gt k)=(k+2)^{-s}P(X>k)=(k+2)−s, E[X]=∑kP(X>k)E[X]=\sum_k P(X\gt k)E[X]=∑k​P(X>k). For this XXX: E[X]=∑k≥0(k+2)−s=ζ(s)−1E[X]=\sum_{k\ge0}(k+2)^{-s}=\zeta(s)-1E[X]=∑k≥0​(k+2)−s=ζ(s)−1, finite only for s>1s\gt1s>1.

    2  Expectation, variance and functions of a discrete RV · Lecture 5

    Theory recap

    A function of a random variable is a random variable. Its PMF comes from grouping the xxx's that map to the same value; its mean does not need that PMF at all (LOTUS). Variance is the mean of one particular function, (X−E[X])2(X-E[X])^2(X−E[X])2.

    Definition: mean and moments

    E[X]=∑x∈Ω′x pX(x)E[X]=\sum_{x\in\Omega'}x\,p_X(x)E[X]=∑x∈Ω′​xpX​(x) (when ∑∣x∣pX(x)<∞\sum|x|p_X(x)\lt\infty∑∣x∣pX​(x)<∞); nnn-th moment E[Xn]=∑xxnpX(x)E[X^n]=\sum_x x^n p_X(x)E[Xn]=∑x​xnpX​(x). For a non-negative XXX the sum may be +∞+\infty+∞ (St. Petersburg).

    Median (course definition): any mmm with P(X≥m)≥12P(X\ge m)\ge\tfrac12P(X≥m)≥21​ and P(X≤m)≥12P(X\le m)\ge\tfrac12P(X≤m)≥21​; equivalently 12≤FX(m)≤12+pX(m)\tfrac12\le F_X(m)\le\tfrac12+p_X(m)21​≤FX​(m)≤21​+pX​(m). Need not be unique.

    PMF of Y = g(X)

    Range ΩY={g(x):x∈ΩX}\Omega_Y=\{g(x):x\in\Omega_X\}ΩY​={g(x):x∈ΩX​} and pY(y)=∑{x: g(x)=y}pX(x).p_Y(y)=\sum_{\{x:\,g(x)=y\}}p_X(x).pY​(y)={x:g(x)=y}∑​pX​(x). If ggg is one-to-one (e.g. Y=aX+bY=aX+bY=aX+b, a≠0a\ne0a=0) then pY(g(x))=pX(x)p_Y(g(x))=p_X(x)pY​(g(x))=pX​(x). Always check ∑ypY(y)=1\sum_y p_Y(y)=1∑y​pY​(y)=1.

    Expected value rule (LOTUS) and linearity

    E[g(X)]=∑xg(x) pX(x).E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)\,p_X(x).E[g(X)]=x∑​g(x)pX​(x). Proof: E[Y]=∑yy pY(y)=∑y∑x:g(x)=yg(x)pX(x)=∑xg(x)pX(x)E[Y]=\sum_y y\,p_Y(y)=\sum_y\sum_{x:g(x)=y}g(x)p_X(x)=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)E[Y]=∑y​ypY​(y)=∑y​∑x:g(x)=y​g(x)pX​(x)=∑x​g(x)pX​(x). Consequences: E[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+b and E[g1(X)+g2(X)]=E[g1(X)]+E[g2(X)]E[g_1(X)+g_2(X)]=E[g_1(X)]+E[g_2(X)]E[g1​(X)+g2​(X)]=E[g1​(X)]+E[g2​(X)]; more generally E[X1+⋯+Xn]=∑E[Xi]E[X_1+\dots+X_n]=\sum E[X_i]E[X1​+⋯+Xn​]=∑E[Xi​] for any random variables (no independence needed).

    Variance

    Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2]\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2], μ=E[X]\mu=E[X]μ=E[X]; σX=Var(X)\sigma_X=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}σX​=Var(X)​.

    • Var(X)=E[X2]−μ2\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-\mu^2Var(X)=E[X2]−μ2 (expand the square, linearity).
    • Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X).
    • Var(X)=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]−E[X]2\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X(X-1)]+E[X]-E[X]^2Var(X)=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]−E[X]2: the factorial-moment route, best for Binomial, Poisson, Geometric.
    • E[(X−α)2]=Var(X)+(μ−α)2E[(X-\alpha)^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X)+(\mu-\alpha)^2E[(X−α)2]=Var(X)+(μ−α)2, minimised at α=μ\alpha=\muα=μ.
    Tail-sum formula

    For XXX with values in {0,1,2,… }\{0,1,2,\dots\}{0,1,2,…}: E[X]=∑k=0∞P(X>k)=∑k=1∞P(X≥k).E[X]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P(X\gt k)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(X\ge k).E[X]=k=0∑∞​P(X>k)=k=1∑∞​P(X≥k). Proof: x=∑k=0x−11x=\sum_{k=0}^{x-1}1x=∑k=0x−1​1, substitute, swap the sums (non-negative terms, Tonelli). For a non-negative XXX in general: E[X]=∫0∞P(X>u) duE[X]=\int_0^\infty P(X\gt u)\,duE[X]=∫0∞​P(X>u)du.

    Watch out

    E[g(X)]≠g(E[X])E[g(X)]\ne g(E[X])E[g(X)]=g(E[X]) in general (e.g. E[X2]≠E[X]2E[X^2]\ne E[X]^2E[X2]=E[X]2, E[2X]≠2E[X]E[2^X]\ne2^{E[X]}E[2X]=2E[X]). And Var(aX+b)\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)Var(aX+b) is a2Var(X)a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)a2Var(X), not aVar(X)+ba\mathrm{Var}(X)+baVar(X)+b.

    Past papers · must-do

    Q1-22.4Prove Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X) 2022 Quiz 1 · Q4 · 5 marks2025 HW 3 Q12★ Must-do

    For a random variable XXX with mean μ\muμ, its variance Var(X)Var(X)Var(X) is defined as E[(X−μ)2]E[(X-\mu)^2]E[(X−μ)2]. Prove that Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X)Var(aX+b)=a^2Var(X)Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X) for arbitrary constants aaa and bbb.

    Same as H25-03.12 (2025 HW 3 Q12). Do it once.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Step 1: shortcut formula. By linearity of expectation (μ\muμ is a constant), Var(X)=E[X2−2μX+μ2]=E[X2]−2μE[X]+μ2=E[X2]−μ2.\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2]=E[X^2]-2\mu E[X]+\mu^2=E[X^2]-\mu^2 .Var(X)=E[X2−2μX+μ2]=E[X2]−2μE[X]+μ2=E[X2]−μ2.

    Step 2: apply it to Y=aX+bY=aX+bY=aX+b. E[Y]=aE[X]+b=aμ+bE[Y]=aE[X]+b=a\mu+bE[Y]=aE[X]+b=aμ+b and E[Y2]=E[a2X2+2abX+b2]=a2E[X2]+2abμ+b2E[Y^2]=E[a^2X^2+2abX+b^2]=a^2E[X^2]+2ab\mu+b^2E[Y2]=E[a2X2+2abX+b2]=a2E[X2]+2abμ+b2. Hence Var(aX+b)=a2E[X2]+2abμ+b2−(a2μ2+2abμ+b2)=a2(E[X2]−μ2).\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2E[X^2]+2ab\mu+b^2-(a^2\mu^2+2ab\mu+b^2)=a^2\big(E[X^2]-\mu^2\big).Var(aX+b)=a2E[X2]+2abμ+b2−(a2μ2+2abμ+b2)=a2(E[X2]−μ2). The b2b^2b2 and 2abμ2ab\mu2abμ terms cancel.

    Directly from the definition (equally valid): aX+b−E[aX+b]=a(X−μ)aX+b-E[aX+b]=a(X-\mu)aX+b−E[aX+b]=a(X−μ), so Var(aX+b)=E[a2(X−μ)2]=a2E[(X−μ)2]\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=E[a^2(X-\mu)^2]=a^2E[(X-\mu)^2]Var(aX+b)=E[a2(X−μ)2]=a2E[(X−μ)2].

    Answer

    Var(aX+b)=a2(E[X2]−E[X]2)=a2 Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2(E[X^2]-E[X]^2)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(aX+b)=a2(E[X2]−E[X]2)=a2Var(X). The shift bbb moves the mean by the same amount, so deviations do not change.

    What the grader checks
    • Linearity of expectation named and used (E[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+b).
    • Both squares expanded, the cancellation of b2b^2b2 and 2abμ2ab\mu2abμ shown, a2a^2a2 factored.
    Q1-22.5Fair die: plot the CDF, mean, variance; prove the tail-sum formula 2022 Quiz 1 · 10-mark Q1 · 10 marks★ Must-do

    Let random variable XXX denote the outcome of a dice. Plot the Cumulative Distribution function (CDF) of XXX. Also find the mean and variance of XXX. Additionally prove that (prove! do not numerically verify. Start with either RHS or LHS and prove the other side.) ∑x∈{1,2,…6}x pX(x)=1+∑x∈{1,2,…6}(1−FX(x))\sum_{x\in\{1,2,\dots6\}} x\,p_X(x)=1+\sum_{x\in\{1,2,\dots6\}}(1-F_X(x))x∈{1,2,…6}∑​xpX​(x)=1+x∈{1,2,…6}∑​(1−FX​(x)) (Hint: Write the CDF on the rhs in terms of PMF.) The RHS is an alternative formula to get the expectation of non-negative random variables using the CDF.

    The general version is Q1-24.1 below.

    Solution · follows the official key

    CDF

    Fair die: pX(k)=16p_X(k)=\tfrac16pX​(k)=61​, k=1,…,6k=1,\dots,6k=1,…,6. Then FX(x)=0F_X(x)=0FX​(x)=0 for x<1x\lt1x<1, FX(x)=z6F_X(x)=\tfrac{z}{6}FX​(x)=6z​ for z≤x<z+1z\le x\lt z+1z≤x<z+1 (z=1,…,5z=1,\dots,5z=1,…,5), and FX(x)=1F_X(x)=1FX​(x)=1 for x≥6x\ge6x≥6: a staircase with jumps of 16\tfrac1661​, closed dot at the left end of each step.

    Mean and variance

    E[X]=1+⋯+66=216=3.5E[X]=\tfrac{1+\dots+6}{6}=\tfrac{21}{6}=3.5E[X]=61+⋯+6​=621​=3.5; E[X2]=1+4+⋯+366=916E[X^2]=\tfrac{1+4+\dots+36}{6}=\tfrac{91}{6}E[X2]=61+4+⋯+36​=691​; Var(X)=916−494=182−14712=3512\mathrm{Var}(X)=\tfrac{91}{6}-\tfrac{49}{4}=\tfrac{182-147}{12}=\tfrac{35}{12}Var(X)=691​−449​=12182−147​=1235​.

    Proof of the identity

    Start from the RHS. 1−FX(x)=P(X>x)=∑k=x+16pX(k)1-F_X(x)=P(X\gt x)=\sum_{k=x+1}^{6}p_X(k)1−FX​(x)=P(X>x)=∑k=x+16​pX​(k). The term x=6x=6x=6 is 0. So 1+∑x=16(1−FX(x))=∑k=16pX(k)+∑x=15∑k=x+16pX(k),1+\sum_{x=1}^{6}(1-F_X(x))=\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_X(k)+\sum_{x=1}^{5}\sum_{k=x+1}^{6}p_X(k),1+x=1∑6​(1−FX​(x))=k=1∑6​pX​(k)+x=1∑5​k=x+1∑6​pX​(k), using 1=∑kpX(k)1=\sum_k p_X(k)1=∑k​pX​(k). In the double sum, a fixed pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) appears once for every xxx with 1≤x≤k−11\le x\le k-11≤x≤k−1, i.e. k−1k-1k−1 times. Adding the single copy from the first sum, pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) appears kkk times in total: 1+∑x(1−FX(x))=∑k=16k pX(k)=LHS.1+\sum_{x}(1-F_X(x))=\sum_{k=1}^{6}k\,p_X(k)=\text{LHS}.1+x∑​(1−FX​(x))=k=1∑6​kpX​(k)=LHS. (Equivalently, write k pX(k)k\,p_X(k)kpX​(k) as kkk copies of pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) in a triangular array and sum the columns: column jjj sums to P(X≥j)P(X\ge j)P(X≥j), and ∑j=16P(X≥j)=1+∑x=15P(X>x)\sum_{j=1}^6P(X\ge j)=1+\sum_{x=1}^{5}P(X\gt x)∑j=16​P(X≥j)=1+∑x=15​P(X>x).)

    Answer

    Staircase CDF with jumps 16\tfrac1661​ at 1,…,61,\dots,61,…,6; E[X]=3.5E[X]=3.5E[X]=3.5, Var(X)=3512≈2.92\mathrm{Var}(X)=\tfrac{35}{12}\approx2.92Var(X)=1235​≈2.92; identity proved by counting how many times each pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) appears.

    What the grader checks
    • CDF plotted as a right-continuous staircase (closed/open endpoints), defined for all real xxx.
    • Mean 3.53.53.5, variance via E[X2]−μ2E[X^2]-\mu^2E[X2]−μ2.
    • A genuine proof: CDF rewritten with the PMF, and the counting of each pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) (no numerical verification).
    Q1-24.1Tail-sum formula E[X] = Σ P(X > i) 2024 Quiz 1 · Q1 · 5 marks★ Must-do

    For a non-negative discrete random variable XXX, prove that E[X]=∑i=0∞P(X>i)E[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}P(X>i)E[X]=∑i=0∞​P(X>i).

    Also PC §3.2.5 Solved Problem 7, B&T supplementary Ch. 2 Problem 10 (the P(N≥i)P(N\ge i)P(N≥i) form), and part (c) of H25-03.7.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Take XXX with values in {0,1,2,… }\{0,1,2,\dots\}{0,1,2,…} (the setting in which the formula holds; see the note below). Definitions: E[X]=∑x=0∞x P(X=x)E[X]=\sum_{x=0}^\infty x\,P(X=x)E[X]=∑x=0∞​xP(X=x) and P(X>i)=∑x=i+1∞P(X=x)P(X\gt i)=\sum_{x=i+1}^{\infty}P(X=x)P(X>i)=∑x=i+1∞​P(X=x).

    Write xxx as a sum. x=∑i=0x−11x=\sum_{i=0}^{x-1}1x=∑i=0x−1​1 for x≥1x\ge1x≥1 (and the x=0x=0x=0 term contributes 0). Then E[X]=∑x=1∞∑i=0x−1P(X=x).E[X]=\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{x-1}P(X=x).E[X]=x=1∑∞​i=0∑x−1​P(X=x).

    Swap the order. The index set is {(x,i):0≤i≤x−1}={(x,i):i≥0, x≥i+1}\{(x,i):0\le i\le x-1\}=\{(x,i): i\ge0,\ x\ge i+1\}{(x,i):0≤i≤x−1}={(x,i):i≥0, x≥i+1}. All terms are non-negative, so the order of summation may be exchanged (Tonelli): E[X]=∑i=0∞∑x=i+1∞P(X=x)=∑i=0∞P(X>i).E[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{x=i+1}^{\infty}P(X=x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}P(X\gt i).E[X]=i=0∑∞​x=i+1∑∞​P(X=x)=i=0∑∞​P(X>i). (If E[X]=∞E[X]=\inftyE[X]=∞ both sides are +∞+\infty+∞.)

    Answer

    E[X]=∑i≥0∑x>iP(X=x)=∑i≥0P(X>i)E[X]=\sum_{i\ge0}\sum_{x\gt i}P(X=x)=\sum_{i\ge0}P(X\gt i)E[X]=∑i≥0​∑x>i​P(X=x)=∑i≥0​P(X>i).

    Non-integer values (accepted by the key)

    If X≥0X\ge0X≥0 takes non-integer values, the same argument with x=∫0xdux=\int_0^x dux=∫0x​du gives E[X]=∫0∞P(X>u) duE[X]=\int_0^\infty P(X\gt u)\,duE[X]=∫0∞​P(X>u)du; the sum ∑iP(X>i)\sum_i P(X\gt i)∑i​P(X>i) then is only a bound (e.g. X≡12X\equiv\tfrac12X≡21​ gives 12\tfrac1221​ vs 111).

    What the grader checks (2024 key)

    • 3 marks: 1 for writing xxx as a sum (or integral), 2 for swapping the sums with the correct limits.
    • 1 mark: final simplification.
    Q1-26.2Entropy as E[−log p_X(X)]; Bernoulli and discrete uniform 2026 Quiz 1 · Q2★ Must-do

    Let XXX be a discrete random variable with probability mass function pX(x)p_X(x)pX​(x). The information content associated with observing the outcome X=xX=xX=x is defined as I(x)=−log⁡pX(x)I(x)=-\log p_X(x)I(x)=−logpX​(x). The entropy of XXX (denoted by H(X)H(X)H(X)) is defined as the expected information content, i.e., H(X)=E[I(X)]H(X)=E[I(X)]H(X)=E[I(X)]. Then show that H(X)=−∑xpX(x)log⁡pX(x)H(X)=-\sum_x p_X(x)\log p_X(x)H(X)=−∑x​pX​(x)logpX​(x). Also obtain the entropy of a i) Bernoulli random variable X∼Bernoulli(p)X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)X∼Bernoulli(p) and ii) a discrete uniform random variable that takes nnn possible values with equal probability.

    Solution · follows the official key

    General formula

    I(X)I(X)I(X) is a function g(X)g(X)g(X) of the discrete random variable XXX, with g(x)=−log⁡pX(x)g(x)=-\log p_X(x)g(x)=−logpX​(x) (defined on the support, where pX(x)>0p_X(x)\gt0pX​(x)>0). By the expected-value rule E[g(X)]=∑xpX(x)g(x)E[g(X)]=\sum_x p_X(x)g(x)E[g(X)]=∑x​pX​(x)g(x), H(X)=E[I(X)]=∑xpX(x)(−log⁡pX(x))=−∑xpX(x)log⁡pX(x).H(X)=E[I(X)]=\sum_x p_X(x)\big(-\log p_X(x)\big)=-\sum_x p_X(x)\log p_X(x).H(X)=E[I(X)]=x∑​pX​(x)(−logpX​(x))=−x∑​pX​(x)logpX​(x).

    i) Bernoulli(p)(p)(p)

    PMF: pX(1)=pp_X(1)=ppX​(1)=p, pX(0)=1−pp_X(0)=1-ppX​(0)=1−p. Information content: I(1)=−log⁡pI(1)=-\log pI(1)=−logp, I(0)=−log⁡(1−p)I(0)=-\log(1-p)I(0)=−log(1−p). Hence H(X)=−plog⁡p−(1−p)log⁡(1−p)H(X)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)H(X)=−plogp−(1−p)log(1−p).

    ii) Uniform on nnn values

    PMF: pX(x)=1np_X(x)=\tfrac1npX​(x)=n1​, x=1,…,nx=1,\dots,nx=1,…,n. Information content: I(x)=−log⁡1n=log⁡nI(x)=-\log\tfrac1n=\log nI(x)=−logn1​=logn for every xxx. Hence H(X)=∑i=1n1nlog⁡n=log⁡nH(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n\tfrac1n\log n=\log nH(X)=∑i=1n​n1​logn=logn.

    Answer

    H(X)=−∑xpX(x)log⁡pX(x)H(X)=-\sum_x p_X(x)\log p_X(x)H(X)=−∑x​pX​(x)logpX​(x); Bernoulli: −plog⁡p−(1−p)log⁡(1−p)-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)−plogp−(1−p)log(1−p); uniform on nnn values: log⁡n\log nlogn.

    What the grader checks
    • Names the expected-value rule (LOTUS) with g=Ig=Ig=I.
    • Each part laid out as PMF → information content → final calculation.

    T26-04.7Y = X mod 3 for a fair die 2026 Tut 4 Q7

    Let XXX be a discrete random variable taking values in {1,2,3,4,5,6}\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}{1,2,3,4,5,6} with P(X=x)=16P(X=x)=\frac{1}{6}P(X=x)=61​, x=1,2,…,6x=1,2,\dots,6x=1,2,…,6. Define Y=X mod 3Y=X \bmod 3Y=Xmod3.

    1,4↦11,4\mapsto11,4↦1; 2,5↦22,5\mapsto22,5↦2; 3,6↦03,6\mapsto03,6↦0. So ΩY={0,1,2}\Omega_Y=\{0,1,2\}ΩY​={0,1,2}.

YYY is uniform on {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}{0,1,2}.

    (d)

    E[Y]=0⋅13+1⋅13+2⋅13=1E[Y]=0\cdot\tfrac13+1\cdot\tfrac13+2\cdot\tfrac13=1E[Y]=0⋅31​+1⋅31​+2⋅31​=1.

    Answer

    Y∈{0,1,2}Y\in\{0,1,2\}Y∈{0,1,2}, each with probability 13\tfrac1331​; P(Y=0)=P(Y=1)=13P(Y=0)=P(Y=1)=\tfrac13P(Y=0)=P(Y=1)=31​; E[Y]=1E[Y]=1E[Y]=1.

    H26-04.1Die scoring 0/5/10/15: PMF, mean, variance 2026 HW 4 Q1

    You roll a fair six-sided die once. If the die shows 1 or 2, you score 0 points; 3 or 4, 5 points; 5, 10 points; 6, 15 points. Let YYY denote your score.

    1. Construct the PMF of YYY.
    2. Find the expected score E[Y]E[Y]E[Y].
    3. Find the variance of YYY.
    Solution · written for this guide

    (a)

    pY(0)=26=13p_Y(0)=\tfrac26=\tfrac13pY​(0)=62​=31​, pY(5)=13p_Y(5)=\tfrac13pY​(5)=31​, pY(10)=16p_Y(10)=\tfrac16pY​(10)=61​, pY(15)=16p_Y(15)=\tfrac16pY​(15)=61​; 0 otherwise.

    (b)

    T25-03.4Median of a fair die 2025 Tut 3 Q4

    The median of a random variable XXX is defined as any number mmm that satisfies both P(X≥m)≥12\mathbb{P}(X\ge m)\ge\frac{1}{2}P(X≥m)≥21​ and P(X≤m)≥12\mathbb{P}(X\le m)\ge\frac{1}{2}P(X≤m)≥21​. Note that the median of XXX is not necessarily unique. Find the median of XXX if XXX is the result of rolling a fair die.

    Part of PC §3.3 Problem 25.

    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    Rewrite the conditions with the CDF: P(X≤m)=FX(m)≥12P(X\le m)=F_X(m)\ge\tfrac12P(X≤m)=FX​(m)≥21​ and P(X≥m)=1−FX(m)+pX(m)≥12P(X\ge m)=1-F_X(m)+p_X(m)\ge\tfrac12P(X≥m)=1−FX​(m)+pX​(m)≥21​, i.e. 12≤FX(m)≤12+pX(m)\tfrac12\le F_X(m)\le\tfrac12+p_X(m)21​≤FX​(m)≤21​+pX​(m).

    • m<3m\lt3m<3: FX(m)≤26<12F_X(m)\le\tfrac26\lt\tfrac12FX​(m)≤62​<21​. Fails.
    • m=3m=3m=3: F=36F=\tfrac36F=63​, and 36≤12+16\tfrac36\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1663​≤21​+61​. Holds.
    • 3<m<43\lt m\lt43<m<4: F=12F=\tfrac12F=21​, pX(m)=0p_X(m)=0pX​(m)=0: 12≤12≤12\tfrac12\le\tfrac12\le\tfrac1221​≤21​≤21​. Holds.
    • m=4m=4m=4: F=46≤12+16F=\tfrac46\le\tfrac12+\tfrac16F=64​≤21​+61​. Holds.
    • m>4m\gt4m>4: P(X≥m)≤26P(X\ge m)\le\tfrac26P(X≥m)≤62​. Fails.
    Answer

    Every m∈[3,4]m\in[3,4]m∈[3,4] is a median.

    T25-03.8Keep or re-roll a die: optimal strategy 2025 Tut 3 Q8

    You roll a single fair six-sided die, and you are paid an amount equal to the value shown. However, you have an option: you can refuse this payment and roll the die a second time. If you opt for the re-roll, you are paid an amount equal to the value of the second roll. What is the optimal strategy to maximize your winnings, and what is the expected payout if you follow this strategy?

    Same as PC §3.3 Problem 24.

    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    If you re-roll, the payout is a fresh fair die with mean 216=3.5\tfrac{21}{6}=3.5621​=3.5. After seeing the first value xxx, keeping gives xxx for sure, re-rolling gives 3.53.53.5 on average. So keep iff x>3.5x\gt3.5x>3.5: keep 4, 5, 6; re-roll 1, 2, 3. (Any strategy is a choice of a set KKK of values to keep, with payout ∑x∈Kx6+6−∣K∣6⋅3.5\sum_{x\in K}\frac{x}{6}+\frac{6-|K|}{6}\cdot3.5∑x∈K​6x​+66−∣K∣​⋅3.5; each xxx adds x−3.56\frac{x-3.5}{6}6x−3.5​, positive exactly for x≥4x\ge4x≥4.)

    Payout W=g(X1,X2)W=g(X_1,X_2)W=g(X1​,X2​): E[W]=P(X1≤3)⋅3.5+∑x=46x6=12⋅72+156=74+52=174E[W]=P(X_1\le3)\cdot3.5+\sum_{x=4}^{6}\tfrac{x}{6}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac72+\tfrac{15}{6}=\tfrac74+\tfrac52=\tfrac{17}{4}E[W]=P(X1​≤3)⋅3.5+∑x=46​6x​=21​⋅27​+615​=47​+25​=417​.

    Answer

    Keep 4–6, re-roll 1–3; E[W]=174=4.25E[W]=\tfrac{17}{4}=4.25E[W]=417​=4.25.

    H25-03.4Alternating arrangements of drawn balls 2025 HW 3 Q4

    A bag contains 8 red balls and 7 blue balls (all identical within color). You draw 4 balls without replacement. Define the random variable XXX = number of ways to arrange the drawn balls in a row such that no two balls of the same color are adjacent.

    1. Find the probability distribution of XXX, and E[X]E[X]E[X].
    2. For general nnn red balls and mmm blue balls, where you draw kkk balls without replacement, provide a general formula for E[X]E[X]E[X].
    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    (a)

    Let RRR be the number of red balls drawn (hypergeometric): P(R=r)=(8r)(74−r)/(154)P(R=r)=\binom8r\binom7{4-r}/\binom{15}4P(R=r)=(r8​)(4−r7​)/(415​). With rrr red and b=4−rb=4-rb=4−r blue, an alternating row needs ∣r−b∣≤1|r-b|\le1∣r−b∣≤1; since r+b=4r+b=4r+b=4 is even this forces r=b=2r=b=2r=b=2, and then exactly two rows work (RBRB, BRBR). So X=g(R)X=g(R)X=g(R) with g(2)=2g(2)=2g(2)=2 and g(r)=0g(r)=0g(r)=0 otherwise: P(X=2)=P(R=2)=(82)(72)(154)=28⋅211365=2865,P(X=0)=3765.P(X=2)=P(R=2)=\frac{\binom82\binom72}{\binom{15}4}=\frac{28\cdot21}{1365}=\frac{28}{65},\qquad P(X=0)=\frac{37}{65}.P(X=2)=P(R=2)=(415​)(28​)(27​)​=136528⋅21​=6528​,P(X=0)=6537​. E[X]=2⋅2865=5665≈0.86E[X]=2\cdot\tfrac{28}{65}=\tfrac{56}{65}\approx0.86E[X]=2⋅6528​=6556​≈0.86.

    (b)

    With rrr red and b=k−rb=k-rb=k−r blue: two alternating rows if r=br=br=b, one if ∣r−b∣=1|r-b|=1∣r−b∣=1 (the majority colour at both ends), none otherwise. Hence

    • kkk even: E[X]=2 (nk/2)(mk/2)(n+mk)E[X]=2\,\dfrac{\binom{n}{k/2}\binom{m}{k/2}}{\binom{n+m}{k}}E[X]=2(kn+m​)(k/2n​)(k/2m​)​.
    • kkk odd: E[X]=(n(k+1)/2)(m(k−1)/2)+(n(k−1)/2)(m(k+1)/2)(n+mk)E[X]=\dfrac{\binom{n}{(k+1)/2}\binom{m}{(k-1)/2}+\binom{n}{(k-1)/2}\binom{m}{(k+1)/2}}{\binom{n+m}{k}}E[X]=(kn+m​)((k+1)/2n​)((k−1)/2m​)+((k−1)/2n​)((k+1)/2m​)​.
    Answer

    (a) P(X=2)=2865P(X=2)=\tfrac{28}{65}P(X=2)=6528​, P(X=0)=3765P(X=0)=\tfrac{37}{65}P(X=0)=6537​, E[X]=5665E[X]=\tfrac{56}{65}E[X]=6556​. (b) The two formulas above.

    H25-03.11St. Petersburg paradox and a capped casino 2025 HW 3 Q11

    A fair coin is tossed at each stage. The pot starts at 1 rupee and is doubled every time a head appears. The first time a tail appears, the game ends and the player wins whatever is in the pot. In short, the player wins 2k−12^{k-1}2k−1 rupees if the coin is tossed kkk times until the first tail appears. What would be a fair price to pay for entering the game?

    2. What is the probability that the player wins more than 65 rupees?

    Y=min⁡(2K−1,230)Y=\min(2^{K-1},2^{30})Y=min(2K−1,230): equal to 2K−12^{K-1}2K−1 for K≤31K\le31K≤31, and 2302^{30}230 for K≥31K\ge31K≥31. So E[Y]=∑k=1302k−12−k+230P(K≥31)=302+230⋅2−30=15+1=16.E[Y]=\sum_{k=1}^{30}2^{k-1}2^{-k}+2^{30}P(K\ge31)=\frac{30}{2}+2^{30}\cdot2^{-30}=15+1=16.E[Y]=k=1∑30​2k−12−k+230P(K≥31)=230​+230⋅2−30=15+1=16.

    H25-03.13Black balls before the white one: $5 per ball, then $2^k 2025 HW 3 Q13

    An urn contains 10 black balls and 1 white ball. The balls are drawn one by one without replacement. The game ends when the white ball is drawn.

The number of black balls drawn first is X=position−1X=\text{position}-1X=position−1, uniform on {0,1,…,10}\{0,1,\dots,10\}{0,1,…,10}: pX(k)=111p_X(k)=\tfrac1{11}pX​(k)=111​.

    LOTUS with g(k)=2kg(k)=2^kg(k)=2k: E[2X]=111∑k=0102k=211−111=204711≈186.09E[2^X]=\tfrac1{11}\sum_{k=0}^{10}2^k=\tfrac{2^{11}-1}{11}=\tfrac{2047}{11}\approx186.09E[2X]=111​∑k=010​2k=11211−1​=112047​≈186.09. (Not 2E[X]=322^{E[X]}=322E[X]=32.)

    (a) $25; (b) $204711≈\tfrac{2047}{11}\approx112047​≈$186.09.

    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    pX(k)=pqk−1p_X(k)=pq^{k-1}pX​(k)=pqk−1, k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dotsk=1,2,…, q=1−pq=1-pq=1−p. LOTUS with g(k)=2−kg(k)=2^{-k}g(k)=2−k: E[2−X]=∑k=1∞2−kpqk−1=p2∑k=1∞(q2)k−1=p2⋅11−q/2=p2−q=p1+p,E[2^{-X}]=\sum_{k=1}^\infty2^{-k}pq^{k-1}=\frac p2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left(\frac q2\right)^{k-1}=\frac p2\cdot\frac{1}{1-q/2}=\frac{p}{2-q}=\frac{p}{1+p},E[2−X]=k=1∑∞​2−kpqk−1=2p​k=1∑∞​(2q​)k−1=2p​⋅1−q/21​=2−qp​=1+pp​, the geometric series converging because 0≤q/2<10\le q/2\lt10≤q/2<1.

    Answer

    E[2−X]=p1+pE[2^{-X}]=\dfrac{p}{1+p}E[2−X]=1+pp​ (compare 2−E[X]=2−1/p2^{-E[X]}=2^{-1/p}2−E[X]=2−1/p, different).

    Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis

    BTS2.9Wheel of fortune: first contestant below contestant 1, E[N] = ∞ B&T Ch. 2 supplementary Problem 9

    Imagine a TV game show where each contestant iii spins an infinitely calibrated wheel of fortune, which assigns him/her some real number with a value between 1 and 100. All values are equally likely and the value obtained by each contestant is independent of the value obtained by any other contestant.

    1. Find P(X1<X2)P(X_1 \lt X_2)P(X1​<X2​).
    2. Find P(X1<X2,X1<X3)P(X_1 \lt X_2, X_1 \lt X_3)P(X1​<X2​,X1​<X3​).
    3. Let NNN be the integer-valued random variable whose value is the index of the first contestant who is assigned a smaller number than contestant 1. (If contestant 1 obtains a smaller value than contestants 2 and 3 but X4<X1X_4\lt X_1X4​<X1​, then N=4N = 4N=4.) Find P(N>n)P(N \gt n)P(N>n) as a function of nnn.
    4. Find E[N]E[N]E[N], assuming an infinite number of contestants.
    Solution · written for this guide

    The values are i.i.d. and continuous, so ties have probability 0 and every ordering of X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ is equally likely (symmetry: permuting i.i.d. variables does not change their joint law).

    (a)

    P(X1<X2)=P(X2<X1)P(X_1\lt X_2)=P(X_2\lt X_1)P(X1​<X2​)=P(X2​<X1​) and they sum to 1: 12\tfrac1221​.

    (b)

    The event says X1X_1X1​ is the smallest of three; each of the three is equally likely to be smallest: 13\tfrac1331​.

    (c)

    For n≥1n\ge1n≥1, N>nN\gt nN>n iff none of contestants 2,…,n2,\dots,n2,…,n is below contestant 1, i.e. X1X_1X1​ is the smallest of X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​: P(N>n)=1nP(N\gt n)=\tfrac1nP(N>n)=n1​ (and P(N>0)=1P(N\gt 0)=1P(N>0)=1; N≥2N\ge2N≥2 always).

    (d)

    NNN is non-negative and integer-valued, so by the tail-sum formula E[N]=∑n=0∞P(N>n)=1+∑n=1∞1n=∞E[N]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty P(N\gt n)=1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1n=\inftyE[N]=n=0∑∞​P(N>n)=1+n=1∑∞​n1​=∞ (harmonic series). NNN is finite with probability 1 (P(N>n)=1/n→0P(N\gt n)=1/n\to0P(N>n)=1/n→0) but has infinite mean. PMF for reference: P(N=n)=1n−1−1n=1n(n−1)P(N=n)=\tfrac1{n-1}-\tfrac1n=\tfrac{1}{n(n-1)}P(N=n)=n−11​−n1​=n(n−1)1​, n≥2n\ge2n≥2.

    Answer

    (a) 12\tfrac1221​; (b) 13\tfrac1331​; (c) P(N>n)=1nP(N\gt n)=\tfrac1nP(N>n)=n1​; (d) E[N]=∞E[N]=\inftyE[N]=∞.

    3  Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson · Lecture 6

    Theory recap

    Counting successes in a fixed number of independent trials gives the binomial; letting the number of trials grow while the success probability shrinks with np=λnp=\lambdanp=λ fixed gives the Poisson. The moment derivations from the PMF are asked almost every year in Quiz 1: learn the factorial-moment trick.

    Indicator / Bernoulli(p)

    1A(ω)=1\mathbf 1_A(\omega)=11A​(ω)=1 if ω∈A\omega\in Aω∈A, else 0; PMF p(1)=P(A)p(1)=\mathbb P(A)p(1)=P(A), p(0)=1−P(A)p(0)=1-\mathbb P(A)p(0)=1−P(A). Bernoulli(p)(p)(p) is the same without naming AAA. E[Xn]=pE[X^n]=pE[Xn]=p for all n≥1n\ge1n≥1 (since Xn=XX^n=XXn=X), so E[X]=pE[X]=pE[X]=p, Var(X)=p−p2=p(1−p)\mathrm{Var}(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)Var(X)=p−p2=p(1−p). E[1A]=P(A)E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A)E[1A​]=P(A).

    Binomial(n, p)

    Number of heads in nnn independent tosses with P(H)=pP(H)=pP(H)=p: pN(k)=(nk)pk(1−p)n−kp_N(k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}pN​(k)=(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k, k=0,…,nk=0,\dots,nk=0,…,n ((nk)\binom nk(kn​) orders, each with probability pkqn−kp^kq^{n-k}pkqn−k by independence). Sums to (p+q)n=1(p+q)^n=1(p+q)n=1 by the binomial theorem.

    E[N]=npE[N]=npE[N]=np, E[N(N−1)]=n(n−1)p2E[N(N-1)]=n(n-1)p^2E[N(N−1)]=n(n−1)p2, E[N2]=n(n−1)p2+npE[N^2]=n(n-1)p^2+npE[N2]=n(n−1)p2+np, Var(N)=np(1−p)\mathrm{Var}(N)=np(1-p)Var(N)=np(1−p). Key identities: k(nk)=n(n−1k−1)k\binom nk=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}k(kn​)=n(k−1n−1​), k(k−1)(nk)=n(n−1)(n−2k−2)k(k-1)\binom nk=n(n-1)\binom{n-2}{k-2}k(k−1)(kn​)=n(n−1)(k−2n−2​).

    Shape: p(k+1)p(k)=n−kk+1⋅p1−p\frac{p(k+1)}{p(k)}=\frac{n-k}{k+1}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}p(k)p(k+1)​=k+1n−k​⋅1−pp​; the mode is ⌊(n+1)p⌋\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor⌊(n+1)p⌋.

    Poisson(λ)

    pX(k)=e−λλkk!p_X(k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}pX​(k)=e−λk!λk​, k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\dotsk=0,1,2,…; sums to e−λeλ=1e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1e−λeλ=1. E[X]=λE[X]=\lambdaE[X]=λ, E[X(X−1)]=λ2E[X(X-1)]=\lambda^2E[X(X−1)]=λ2, Var(X)=λ\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambdaVar(X)=λ.

    Poisson limit theorem: if n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, p→0p\to0p→0 with np=λnp=\lambdanp=λ fixed, then (nk)pk(1−p)n−k→e−λλkk!\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\to e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k→e−λk!λk​ for each fixed kkk.

    Series you will need
    • Geometric: ∑k≥0xk=11−x\sum_{k\ge0}x^k=\frac1{1-x}∑k≥0​xk=1−x1​, ∣x∣<1|x|\lt1∣x∣<1; finite: ∑k=0nrk=rn+1−1r−1\sum_{k=0}^{n}r^k=\frac{r^{n+1}-1}{r-1}∑k=0n​rk=r−1rn+1−1​.
    • Differentiate once: ∑k≥1kxk−1=1(1−x)2\sum_{k\ge1}kx^{k-1}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}∑k≥1​kxk−1=(1−x)21​; twice: ∑k≥2k(k−1)xk−2=2(1−x)3\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)x^{k-2}=\frac{2}{(1-x)^3}∑k≥2​k(k−1)xk−2=(1−x)32​; hence ∑k≥1k2xk−1=1+x(1−x)3\sum_{k\ge1}k^2x^{k-1}=\frac{1+x}{(1-x)^3}∑k≥1​k2xk−1=(1−x)31+x​.
    • Exponential: ∑k≥0λkk!=eλ\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}=e^\lambda∑k≥0​k!λk​=eλ; (1−λn)n→e−λ\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\to e^{-\lambda}(1−nλ​)n→e−λ.
    • Binomial theorem: ∑k=0n(nk)akbn−k=(a+b)n\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a^kb^{n-k}=(a+b)^n∑k=0n​(kn​)akbn−k=(a+b)n.

    Term-by-term differentiation of a power series is valid inside its radius of convergence (∣x∣<1|x|\lt1∣x∣<1 here).

    Watch out

    Dropping (nk)\binom nk(kn​) from the binomial PMF (it counts the orders). For moment derivations, start the sum where the factor kkk or k(k−1)k(k-1)k(k−1) stops being 0, and re-index before using the binomial theorem or eλe^\lambdaeλ.

    Q1-25.2First two moments (and variance) of Binomial(n, p) 2025 Quiz 1 · Q2 · 10 marks2024 Quiz 1 · Q4 (Binomial part) · 2.5 marks★ Must-do

    Let XXX be a Binomial random variable with parameters nnn and ppp. Derive expression for the first two moments of XXX.

    Same as Q1-24.4b (2024 Quiz 1 Q4: "Let YYY denote a Binomial random variable with parameters nnn and ppp. Derive the expression for its variance"). PC §3.2.5 Solved Problem 6 is the mean part. Do it once, and finish with the variance.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Setup. pX(k)=(nk)pkqn−kp_X(k)=\binom nk p^k q^{n-k}pX​(k)=(kn​)pkqn−k, k=0,1,…,nk=0,1,\dots,nk=0,1,…,n, q=1−pq=1-pq=1−p.

    First moment

    The k=0k=0k=0 term vanishes. Use k(nk)=kn!k!(n−k)!=n(n−1)!(k−1)!(n−k)!=n(n−1k−1)k\binom nk=k\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}=n\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}k(kn​)=kk!(n−k)!n!​=n(k−1)!(n−k)!(n−1)!​=n(k−1n−1​): E[X]=∑k=1nn(n−1k−1)pkqn−k=np∑j=0n−1(n−1j)pjq(n−1)−j=np(p+q)n−1=np,E[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}n\binom{n-1}{k-1}p^kq^{n-k}=np\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}p^{j}q^{(n-1)-j}=np(p+q)^{n-1}=np,E[X]=k=1∑n​n(k−1n−1​)pkqn−k=npj=0∑n−1​(jn−1​)pjq(n−1)−j=np(p+q)n−1=np, with j=k−1j=k-1j=k−1 and the binomial theorem.

    Second moment

    Split k2=k(k−1)+kk^2=k(k-1)+kk2=k(k−1)+k, so E[X2]=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]E[X^2]=E[X(X-1)]+E[X]E[X2]=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]. The terms k=0,1k=0,1k=0,1 of E[X(X−1)]E[X(X-1)]E[X(X−1)] vanish; k(k−1)(nk)=n(n−1)(n−2k−2)k(k-1)\binom nk=n(n-1)\binom{n-2}{k-2}k(k−1)(kn​)=n(n−1)(k−2n−2​): E[X(X−1)]=n(n−1)p2∑k=2n(n−2k−2)pk−2qn−k=n(n−1)p2(p+q)n−2=n(n−1)p2.E[X(X-1)]=n(n-1)p^2\sum_{k=2}^{n}\binom{n-2}{k-2}p^{k-2}q^{n-k}=n(n-1)p^2(p+q)^{n-2}=n(n-1)p^2.E[X(X−1)]=n(n−1)p2k=2∑n​(k−2n−2​)pk−2qn−k=n(n−1)p2(p+q)n−2=n(n−1)p2. Hence E[X2]=n(n−1)p2+npE[X^2]=n(n-1)p^2+npE[X2]=n(n−1)p2+np.

    Variance

    Var(X)=E[X2]−E[X]2=n2p2−np2+np−n2p2=np(1−p)\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2=n^2p^2-np^2+np-n^2p^2=np(1-p)Var(X)=E[X2]−E[X]2=n2p2−np2+np−n2p2=np(1−p).

    Answer

    E[X]=npE[X]=npE[X]=np, E[X2]=n(n−1)p2+npE[X^2]=n(n-1)p^2+npE[X2]=n(n−1)p2+np, Var(X)=np(1−p)\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)Var(X)=np(1−p).

    Other methods in the keys

    Differentiate in ppp (2024 key): differentiate ∑k(nk)pk(1−p)n−k=1\sum_k\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}=1∑k​(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k=1 to get ∑k(nk)pkqn−k(kp−n−kq)=0\sum_k\binom nk p^kq^{n-k}\left(\frac kp-\frac{n-k}{q}\right)=0∑k​(kn​)pkqn−k(pk​−qn−k​)=0, i.e. E[X]p=n−E[X]q⇒E[X]=np\frac{E[X]}{p}=\frac{n-E[X]}{q}\Rightarrow E[X]=nppE[X]​=qn−E[X]​⇒E[X]=np; differentiating once more gives E[X2]E[X^2]E[X2]. Sum of Bernoullis: X=∑i=1nXiX=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iX=∑i=1n​Xi​, XiX_iXi​ i.i.d. Bernoulli(p)(p)(p); linearity gives npnpnp, and additivity of variance for independent terms gives np(1−p)np(1-p)np(1−p) (the 2025 key notes this uses material from later in the course).

    What the grader checks

    • Split k2=k(k−1)+kk^2=k(k-1)+kk2=k(k−1)+k and the second identity.

    MS23.B2bMean and variance of Poisson(λ) from the PMF 2023 Midsem · 10-mark Q2 (Poisson part) · 5 marks★ Must-do

    Let XXX be a uniform random variable with support [a,b][a, b][a,b]. Let YYY be Poisson random variable with parameter λ\lambdaλ. Derive the expression for the mean and variance of XXX and YYY.

    Only the Poisson part belongs here (the uniform part is topic 3). Same as PC §3.2.5 Solved Problem 8 (variance) and parts (b), (c) of T25-03.1.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Setup. pY(y)=e−λλyy!p_Y(y)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^y}{y!}pY​(y)=e−λy!λy​, y=0,1,2,…y=0,1,2,\dotsy=0,1,2,…, λ>0\lambda\gt0λ>0.

    Mean

    The y=0y=0y=0 term is 0; yy!=1(y−1)!\frac{y}{y!}=\frac{1}{(y-1)!}y!y​=(y−1)!1​; put j=y−1j=y-1j=y−1: E[Y]=∑y=1∞y e−λλyy!=λe−λ∑j=0∞λjj!=λe−λeλ=λ.E[Y]=\sum_{y=1}^\infty y\,e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^y}{y!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=\lambda.E[Y]=y=1∑∞​ye−λy!λy​=λe−λj=0∑∞​j!λj​=λe−λeλ=λ.

    Variance via the factorial moment

    The terms y=0,1y=0,1y=0,1 vanish; y(y−1)y!=1(y−2)!\frac{y(y-1)}{y!}=\frac{1}{(y-2)!}y!y(y−1)​=(y−2)!1​: E[Y(Y−1)]=λ2e−λ∑y=2∞λy−2(y−2)!=λ2.E[Y(Y-1)]=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum_{y=2}^\infty\frac{\lambda^{y-2}}{(y-2)!}=\lambda^2.E[Y(Y−1)]=λ2e−λy=2∑∞​(y−2)!λy−2​=λ2. So E[Y2]=E[Y(Y−1)]+E[Y]=λ2+λE[Y^2]=E[Y(Y-1)]+E[Y]=\lambda^2+\lambdaE[Y2]=E[Y(Y−1)]+E[Y]=λ2+λ and Var(Y)=λ2+λ−λ2=λ\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambdaVar(Y)=λ2+λ−λ2=λ.

    Answer

    E[Y]=λE[Y]=\lambdaE[Y]=λ, Var(Y)=λ\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\lambdaVar(Y)=λ (and E[Y2]=λ2+λE[Y^2]=\lambda^2+\lambdaE[Y2]=λ2+λ).

    Q1-23.6Which airline is more overbooked? (Binomial show-ups) 2023 Quiz 1 · Q6 · 5 marks★ Must-do

    Airlines find that any passenger who books a seat, often fails to turn up with probability 110\frac{1}{10}101​. Indigo always sells 10 tickets for their 9 seat aeroplane. AirIndia sells 20 tickets for their 18 seat aeroplane. Which airline is more overbooked. Justify your answer. (Hint: Invoke Binomial B(n,p)B(n,p)B(n,p) random variable)

    Solution · follows the official key

    Criterion. An airline is "more overbooked" if the probability that more passengers show up than there are seats is larger.

    Model. Passengers show up independently with probability 0.90.90.9. Indigo: N∼B(10,0.9)N\sim B(10,0.9)N∼B(10,0.9); AirIndia: M∼B(20,0.9)M\sim B(20,0.9)M∼B(20,0.9); P(N=k)=(10k)0.9k0.110−kP(N=k)=\binom{10}{k}0.9^k0.1^{10-k}P(N=k)=(k10​)0.9k0.110−k, similarly for MMM.

    Indigo. P(N>9)=P(N=10)=0.910≈0.3487P(N\gt9)=P(N=10)=0.9^{10}\approx0.3487P(N>9)=P(N=10)=0.910≈0.3487.

    AirIndia. P(M>18)=P(M=19)+P(M=20)=(2019)0.919(0.1)+0.920=0.919(2+0.9)≈0.2702+0.1216=0.3917P(M\gt18)=P(M=19)+P(M=20)=\binom{20}{19}0.9^{19}(0.1)+0.9^{20}=0.9^{19}(2+0.9)\approx0.2702+0.1216=0.3917P(M>18)=P(M=19)+P(M=20)=(1920​)0.919(0.1)+0.920=0.919(2+0.9)≈0.2702+0.1216=0.3917.

    Answer

    0.349<0.3920.349\lt0.3920.349<0.392: AirIndia is more overbooked.

    What the grader checks (2023 key)
    • 1: defines "more overbooked" as a larger probability that show-ups exceed seats.
    • 1: binomial model with success probability 9/10, PMF written.
    • 1: Indigo 0.9100.9^{10}0.910. 1.5: AirIndia, both terms. 0.5: comparison and conclusion.

    T26-04.212 throws with hit probability 2/3 2026 Tut 4 Q2

    You are playing a target-throwing game consisting of 12 throws. In each throw, you have a probability of 23\frac{2}{3}32​ of successfully hitting the target. Let YYY denote the total number of successful throws.

    1. Identify the probability distribution of YYY and write its PMF.
    2. Find the expected number of successful throws, E[Y]E[Y]E[Y].
    3. Find the variance of YYY.
    Solution · written for this guide

    (a)

    Assuming throws are independent with the same hit probability, YYY counts successes in 12 Bernoulli(23)(\tfrac23)(32​) trials: Y∼Y\simY∼ Binomial(12,23)(12,\tfrac23)(12,32​), pY(k)=(12k)(23)k(13)12−k,k=0,1,…,12.p_Y(k)=\binom{12}{k}\left(\tfrac23\right)^k\left(\tfrac13\right)^{12-k},\quad k=0,1,\dots,12.pY​(k)=(k12​)(32​)k(31​)12−k,k=0,1,…,12.

    (b), (c)

    E[Y]=np=12⋅23=8E[Y]=np=12\cdot\tfrac23=8E[Y]=np=12⋅32​=8; Var(Y)=np(1−p)=12⋅23⋅13=83\mathrm{Var}(Y)=np(1-p)=12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac83Var(Y)=np(1−p)=12⋅32​⋅31​=38​.

    Answer

    Binomial(12,23)(12,\tfrac23)(12,32​); E[Y]=8E[Y]=8E[Y]=8, Var(Y)=83\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\tfrac83Var(Y)=38​.

    T26-04.3Gambler's ±1 walk: parity, range, PMF, mean, variance 2026 Tut 4 Q3

    A gambler tosses a coin nnn times, each toss independent of the others. The outcome of the iii-th toss is XiX_iXi​ with P(Xi=+1)=pP(X_i=+1)=pP(Xi​=+1)=p, P(Xi=−1)=1−p=qP(X_i=-1)=1-p=qP(Xi​=−1)=1−p=q, 0<p<10\lt p\lt10<p<1. Total earnings are Yn=∑i=1nXiY_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_iYn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, n≥1n\ge 1n≥1.

    1. Find E[Xi]E[X_i]E[Xi​], Var(Xi)Var(X_i)Var(Xi​).
    2. What is the parity (odd/even) of Y2kY_{2k}Y2k​ where k∈Nk\in\mathbb{N}k∈N and 2k≤n2k\le n2k≤n? What about Y2k+1Y_{2k+1}Y2k+1​ where 2k+1≤n2k+1\le n2k+1≤n?
    3. Find the possible set of values of YnY_nYn​.
    4. Find the PMF of YnY_nYn​, E[Yn]E[Y_n]E[Yn​], Var(Yn)Var(Y_n)Var(Yn​).
    Solution · written for this guide

    (a)

    E[Xi]=p−q=2p−1E[X_i]=p-q=2p-1E[Xi​]=p−q=2p−1. Xi2=1X_i^2=1Xi2​=1, so E[Xi2]=1E[X_i^2]=1E[Xi2​]=1 and Var(Xi)=1−(2p−1)2=4p−4p2=4pq\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=1-(2p-1)^2=4p-4p^2=4pqVar(Xi​)=1−(2p−1)2=4p−4p2=4pq.

    Key step

    T25-03.1Poisson PMF: consistency, mean, variance 2025 Tut 3 Q1

    Let XXX be a Poisson random variable with parameter λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, pX(k)=e−λλkk!p_X(k)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}pX​(k)=k!e−λλk​, k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\dotsk=0,1,2,…

    1. Show that pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) is consistent.
    2. Derive the mean (expected value) of XXX.
    3. Derive the variance of XXX.
    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    (a)

    pX(k)≥0p_X(k)\ge0pX​(k)≥0 since e−λ>0e^{-\lambda}\gt0e−λ>0, λk≥0\lambda^k\ge0λk≥0, k!>0k!\gt0k!>0. And ∑k≥0e−λλkk!=e−λeλ=1\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1∑k≥0​e−λk!λk​=e−λeλ=1 (exponential series).

    (b)

    E[X]=∑k≥1e−λλk(k−1)!=λe−λ∑j≥0λjj!=λE[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}=\lambdaE[X]=∑k≥1​e−λ(k−1)!λk​=λe−λ∑j≥0​j!λj​=λ.

    (c)

    Write k2=k((k−1)+1)k^2=k\big((k-1)+1\big)k2=k((k−1)+1): E[X2]=∑k≥1[(k−1)+1]e−λλk(k−1)!=λ2e−λ∑k≥2λk−2(k−2)!+λ=λ2+λE[X^2]=\sum_{k\ge1}[(k-1)+1]e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!}=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{\lambda^{k-2}}{(k-2)!}+\lambda=\lambda^2+\lambdaE[X2]=∑k≥1​[(k−1)+1]e−λ(k−1)!λk​=λ2e−λ∑k≥2​(k−2)!λk−2​+λ=λ2+λ. So Var(X)=λ2+λ−λ2=λ\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambdaVar(X)=λ2+λ−λ2=λ.

    Answer

    Valid PMF; E[X]=λE[X]=\lambdaE[X]=λ, Var(X)=λ\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambdaVar(X)=λ. (Mean and variance are the same derivation as MS23.B2b.)

    Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis

    BT2.9Shape of the binomial PMF: rises up to k* = ⌊(n+1)p⌋ B&T Ch. 2 Problem 9

    Form of the binomial PMF. Consider a binomial random variable XXX with parameters nnn and ppp. Let k∗k^*k∗ be the largest integer that is less than or equal to (n+1)p(n+1)p(n+1)p. Show that the PMF pX(k)p_X(k)pX​(k) is monotonically nondecreasing with kkk in the range from 0 to k∗k^*k∗, and is monotonically decreasing with kkk for k≥k∗k\ge k^*k≥k∗.

    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    Take 0<p<10\lt p\lt10<p<1. For k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,nk=1,…,n, compare consecutive masses: pX(k)pX(k−1)=(nk)pkqn−k(nk−1)pk−1qn−k+1=n−k+1k⋅pq.\frac{p_X(k)}{p_X(k-1)}=\frac{\binom nk p^kq^{n-k}}{\binom n{k-1}p^{k-1}q^{n-k+1}}=\frac{n-k+1}{k}\cdot\frac pq .pX​(k−1)pX​(k)​=(k−1n​)pk−1qn−k+1(kn​)pkqn−k​=kn−k+1​⋅qp​. This ratio is ≥1\ge1≥1 iff (n−k+1)p≥kq=k(1−p)(n-k+1)p\ge kq=k(1-p)(n−k+1)p≥kq=k(1−p) iff (n+1)p≥k(n+1)p\ge k(n+1)p≥k.

    • For 1≤k≤k∗1\le k\le k^*1≤k≤k∗: k≤k∗≤(n+1)pk\le k^*\le(n+1)pk≤k∗≤(n+1)p, so pX(k)≥pX(k−1)p_X(k)\ge p_X(k-1)pX​(k)≥pX​(k−1): nondecreasing on 0,…,k∗0,\dots,k^*0,…,k∗.
    • For k≥k∗+1k\ge k^*+1k≥k∗+1: k>(n+1)pk\gt(n+1)pk>(n+1)p (since k∗k^*k∗ is the largest integer ≤(n+1)p\le(n+1)p≤(n+1)p), so pX(k)<pX(k−1)p_X(k)\lt p_X(k-1)pX​(k)<pX​(k−1): strictly decreasing from k∗k^*k∗ on.
    Answer

    The ratio pX(k)pX(k−1)=(n−k+1)pk(1−p)\frac{p_X(k)}{p_X(k-1)}=\frac{(n-k+1)p}{k(1-p)}pX​(k−1)pX​(k)​=k(1−p)(n−k+1)p​ is ≥1\ge1≥1 exactly when k≤(n+1)pk\le(n+1)pk≤(n+1)p; so the PMF peaks at k∗=⌊(n+1)p⌋k^*=\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloork∗=⌊(n+1)p⌋ (two equal peaks k∗−1,k∗k^*-1,k^*k∗−1,k∗ when (n+1)p(n+1)p(n+1)p is an integer).

    BT2.12Poisson limit of the binomial (np = λ fixed) B&T Ch. 2 Problem 12*

    Justification of the Poisson approximation property. Consider the PMF of a binomial random variable with parameters nnn and ppp. Show that asymptotically, as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, p→0p\to0p→0, while npnpnp is fixed at a given value λ\lambdaλ, this PMF approaches the PMF of a Poisson random variable with parameter λ\lambdaλ.

    Fix k≥0k\ge0k≥0 and put p=λ/np=\lambda/np=λ/n (n>λn\gt\lambdan>λ). Then pX(k)=n!(n−k)! k!λknk(1−λn)n−k=n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)nk⋅λkk!⋅(1−λn)n⋅(1−λn)−k.p_X(k)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!\,k!}\frac{\lambda^k}{n^k}\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{n-k}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k}\cdot\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}\cdot\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{n}\cdot\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-k}.pX​(k)=(n−k)!k!n!​nkλk​(1−nλ​)n−k=nkn(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)​⋅k!λk​⋅(1−nλ​)n⋅(1−nλ​)−k. As n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ with kkk fixed:

    • n−k+jn→1\frac{n-k+j}{n}\to1nn−k+j​→1 for each j=1,…,kj=1,\dots,kj=1,…,k, so the first factor (a product of kkk such terms) →1\to1→1;
    • (1−λn)n→e−λ\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\to e^{-\lambda}(1−nλ​)n→e−λ;
    • (1−λn)−k→1\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-k}\to1(1−nλ​)−k→1 (fixed power of something →1\to1→1).

    (nk)(λn)k(1−λn)n−k⟶e−λλkk!\displaystyle\binom nk\left(\tfrac\lambda n\right)^k\left(1-\tfrac\lambda n\right)^{n-k}\longrightarrow e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}(kn​)(nλ​)k(1−nλ​)n−k⟶e−λk!λk​ for every fixed kkk: Binomial(n,λ/n)→(n,\lambda/n)\to(n,λ/n)→ Poisson(λ)(\lambda)(λ).

    Use

    B&T Problem 2: probability that exactly one of 500 other guests shares your birthday: exact 500⋅1365(364365)499≈0.3484500\cdot\frac1{365}\left(\frac{364}{365}\right)^{499}\approx0.3484500⋅3651​(365364​)499≈0.3484; Poisson with λ=500/365\lambda=500/365λ=500/365: λe−λ≈0.3481\lambda e^{-\lambda}\approx0.3481λe−λ≈0.3481.

    4  Geometric distribution and memorylessness · Lecture 6

    Theory recap

    "Repeat independent trials until the first success" gives the geometric distribution. Its tail is a pure power, which makes it memoryless, and its moments come from differentiating the geometric series. The mean/variance derivation was asked in Quiz 1 in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

    Geometric(p) on {1, 2, ...}

    NNN = number of trials up to and including the first success: pN(k)=(1−p)k−1pp_N(k)=(1-p)^{k-1}ppN​(k)=(1−p)k−1p, k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dotsk=1,2,… (one order only: k−1k-1k−1 failures then a success; no binomial coefficient).

    • Tail: P(N>k)=(1−p)kP(N\gt k)=(1-p)^kP(N>k)=(1−p)k (the first kkk trials fail); CDF FN(k)=1−(1−p)kF_N(k)=1-(1-p)^kFN​(k)=1−(1−p)k.
    • E[N]=1pE[N]=\frac1pE[N]=p1​, E[N2]=2−pp2E[N^2]=\frac{2-p}{p^2}E[N2]=p22−p​, E[N(N−1)]=2(1−p)p2E[N(N-1)]=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}E[N(N−1)]=p22(1−p)​, Var(N)=1−pp2\mathrm{Var}(N)=\frac{1-p}{p^2}Var(N)=p21−p​.
    • Tail-sum check: E[N]=∑k≥0(1−p)k=1pE[N]=\sum_{k\ge0}(1-p)^k=\frac1pE[N]=∑k≥0​(1−p)k=p1​.
    Memoryless property

    P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k+m)P(N>k)=(1−p)k+m(1−p)k=(1−p)m=P(N>m)P(N\gt k+m\mid N\gt k)=\frac{P(N\gt k+m)}{P(N\gt k)}=\frac{(1-p)^{k+m}}{(1-p)^k}=(1-p)^m=P(N\gt m)P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k)P(N>k+m)​=(1−p)k(1−p)k+m​=(1−p)m=P(N>m).

    Having waited kkk trials without success, the remaining wait is again Geometric(p)(p)(p): the trials after time kkk are independent of the first kkk. Among distributions on {1,2,… }\{1,2,\dots\}{1,2,…}, only the geometric is memoryless (exponential in the continuous case). In particular the gap between the 1st and 2nd success is Geometric(p)(p)(p) as well.

    Recognising a geometric
    • Each "round" ends the experiment with the same probability sss, independently of earlier rounds ⇒ number of rounds ∼\sim∼ Geometric(s)(s)(s), whatever happens inside a round.
    • Who wins in the final round: P(A wins∣round ends)=P(A wins a round)sP(\text{A wins}\mid\text{round ends})=\frac{P(\text{A wins a round})}{s}P(A wins∣round ends)=sP(A wins a round)​.
    • Shifted versions: X=Y+cX=Y+cX=Y+c has E[X]=E[Y]+cE[X]=E[Y]+cE[X]=E[Y]+c, Var(X)=Var(Y)\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{Var}(Y)Var(X)=Var(Y).
    Watch out

    Some books count failures before the first success (support {0,1,… }\{0,1,\dots\}{0,1,…}, mean 1−pp\frac{1-p}{p}p1−p​). This course uses trials, support {1,2,… }\{1,2,\dots\}{1,2,…}, mean 1p\frac1pp1​. State the support you use.

    Past papers · must-do

    Q1-24.2Mean, second moment and variance of Geometric(p) 2024 Quiz 1 · Q2 · 5 marks2023 Quiz 1 · Q2 · 5 marks2022 Quiz 1 · Q2 · 5 marks★ Must-do

    Consider a Geometric random variable XXX with parameter ppp. Derive the expression for its mean, second moment and variance.

    Same as Q1-22.2 and Q1-23.2 ("A geometric random variable XXX with parameter ppp has PMF pX(k)=(1−p)k−1pp_X(k)=(1-p)^{k-1}ppX​(k)=(1−p)k−1p. Derive the expression for its mean and variance"), PC §3.3 Problem 17 and B&T Ch. 2 Problem 20. Do it once.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Setup. P(X=k)=qk−1pP(X=k)=q^{k-1}pP(X=k)=qk−1p, k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dotsk=1,2,…, 0<p≤10\lt p\le10<p≤1, q=1−pq=1-pq=1−p. For ∣x∣<1|x|\lt1∣x∣<1, ∑k≥0xk=11−x\sum_{k\ge0}x^k=\frac1{1-x}∑k≥0​xk=1−x1​; differentiating term by term (valid inside the radius of convergence) gives ∑k≥1kxk−1=1(1−x)2,∑k≥2k(k−1)xk−2=2(1−x)3.\sum_{k\ge1}kx^{k-1}=\frac1{(1-x)^2},\qquad \sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)x^{k-2}=\frac{2}{(1-x)^3}.k≥1∑​kxk−1=(1−x)21​,k≥2∑​k(k−1)xk−2=(1−x)32​.

    Mean

    E[X]=∑k≥1k qk−1p=p∑k≥1kqk−1=p(1−q)2=pp2=1p.E[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}k\,q^{k-1}p=p\sum_{k\ge1}kq^{k-1}=\frac{p}{(1-q)^2}=\frac{p}{p^2}=\frac1p .E[X]=k≥1∑​kqk−1p=pk≥1∑​kqk−1=(1−q)2p​=p2p​=p1​.

    Second moment

    Multiply ∑k≥1kxk=x(1−x)2\sum_{k\ge1}kx^{k}=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}∑k≥1​kxk=(1−x)2x​ and differentiate: ∑k≥1k2xk−1=ddxx(1−x)2=1+x(1−x)3\sum_{k\ge1}k^2x^{k-1}=\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}=\frac{1+x}{(1-x)^3}∑k≥1​k2xk−1=dxd​(1−x)2x​=(1−x)31+x​. Hence E[X2]=p∑k≥1k2qk−1=p⋅1+q(1−q)3=2−pp2.E[X^2]=p\sum_{k\ge1}k^2q^{k-1}=p\cdot\frac{1+q}{(1-q)^3}=\frac{2-p}{p^2}.E[X2]=pk≥1∑​k2qk−1=p⋅(1−q)31+q​=p22−p​. (2023 key route: E[X(X−1)]=pq∑k≥2k(k−1)qk−2=2pqp3=2(1−p)p2E[X(X-1)]=pq\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)q^{k-2}=\frac{2pq}{p^3}=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}E[X(X−1)]=pq∑k≥2​k(k−1)qk−2=p32pq​=p22(1−p)​, then E[X2]=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]=2−2p+pp2E[X^2]=E[X(X-1)]+E[X]=\frac{2-2p+p}{p^2}E[X2]=E[X(X−1)]+E[X]=p22−2p+p​.)

    Variance

    Var(X)=E[X2]−E[X]2=2−pp2−1p2=1−pp2.\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2=\frac{2-p}{p^2}-\frac1{p^2}=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.Var(X)=E[X2]−E[X]2=p22−p​−p21​=p21−p​.

    Answer

    E[X]=1pE[X]=\frac1pE[X]=p1​, E[X2]=2−pp2E[X^2]=\frac{2-p}{p^2}E[X2]=p22−p​, Var(X)=1−pp2\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{1-p}{p^2}Var(X)=p21−p​.

    Alternative in the 2024 key (total expectation)

    Condition on the first trial: with probability ppp, X=1X=1X=1; otherwise the process restarts, X=1+X′X=1+X'X=1+X′ with X′X'X′ an independent copy. So E[X]=p+q(1+E[X])⇒E[X]=1pE[X]=p+q(1+E[X])\Rightarrow E[X]=\frac1pE[X]=p+q(1+E[X])⇒E[X]=p1​, and E[X2]=p+qE[(1+X)2]=p+q(1+2p+E[X2])⇒E[X2]=2−pp2E[X^2]=p+qE[(1+X)^2]=p+q(1+\frac2p+E[X^2])\Rightarrow E[X^2]=\frac{2-p}{p^2}E[X2]=p+qE[(1+X)2]=p+q(1+p2​+E[X2])⇒E[X2]=p22−p​. (Conditioning is topic 5.)

    What the grader checks
    • 2024: mean 2 (1 setup, 1 result), second moment 2 (1 setup, 1 result), variance 1.
    • 2023: mean = 0.5 setup, 0.5 factor ppp, 1 series sum, 0.5 final; variance = 0.5 formula, 0.5 split E[X(X−1)]+E[X]−E[X]2E[X(X-1)]+E[X]-E[X]^2E[X(X−1)]+E[X]−E[X]2, 1 series, 0.5 final.
    • Always state the support k≥1k\ge1k≥1 and why the differentiated series converges (q<1q\lt1q<1).

    H26-04.2First +1 of the gambler: geometric, memoryless, gap N₂ − N₁ 2026 HW 4 Q2

    (Gambler: each toss is +1+1+1 with probability ppp and −1-1−1 with probability q=1−pq=1-pq=1−p, independently.) Suppose the gambler keeps tossing the coin indefinitely. Let NNN be the first time the gambler sees a +1+1+1.

    1. Model this as a geometric random variable.
    2. Find the PMF of NNN, E[N]E[N]E[N].
    3. Prove the memoryless property P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>m)P(N>k+m\mid N>k)=P(N>m)P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>m).
    4. Let N1N_1N1​ be the first time that a +1+1+1 appears, and N2N_2N2​ be the second time it appears. What kind of random variable is N2−N1N_2-N_1N2​−N1​? (Hint: use the memoryless property.)

    Part (c) is also PC §3.3 Problem 9.

    Solution · written for this guide

    (a), (b)

    Each toss is an independent Bernoulli trial with "success" = +1+1+1, probability ppp. N=kN=kN=k iff tosses 1,…,k−11,\dots,k-11,…,k−1 are −1-1−1 and toss kkk is +1+1+1; by independence pN(k)=qk−1p,k=1,2,…,p_N(k)=q^{k-1}p,\qquad k=1,2,\dots,pN​(k)=qk−1p,k=1,2,…, so N∼N\simN∼ Geometric(p)(p)(p) and E[N]=p∑k≥1kqk−1=p(1−q)2=1pE[N]=p\sum_{k\ge1}kq^{k-1}=\frac{p}{(1-q)^2}=\frac1pE[N]=p∑k≥1​kqk−1=(1−q)2p​=p1​.

    (c)

    P(N>j)=P(first j tosses are −1)=qjP(N\gt j)=P(\text{first }j\text{ tosses are }-1)=q^jP(N>j)=P(first j tosses are −1)=qj. Since {N>k+m}⊆{N>k}\{N\gt k+m\}\subseteq\{N\gt k\}{N>k+m}⊆{N>k}, P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k+m)P(N>k)=qk+mqk=qm=P(N>m).P(N\gt k+m\mid N\gt k)=\frac{P(N\gt k+m)}{P(N\gt k)}=\frac{q^{k+m}}{q^k}=q^m=P(N\gt m).P(N>k+m∣N>k)=P(N>k)P(N>k+m)​=qkqk+m​=qm=P(N>m).

    (d)

    For m≥1m\ge1m≥1, split on the value of N1N_1N1​ (disjoint events): P(N2−N1=m)=∑k≥1P(N1=k, tosses k+1,…,k+m−1 are −1, toss k+m is +1).P(N_2-N_1=m)=\sum_{k\ge1}P(N_1=k,\ \text{tosses }k+1,\dots,k+m-1\text{ are }-1,\ \text{toss }k+m\text{ is }+1).P(N2​−N1​=m)=k≥1∑​P(N1​=k, tosses k+1,…,k+m−1 are −1, toss k+m is +1). The event {N1=k}\{N_1=k\}{N1​=k} depends only on tosses 1,…,k1,\dots,k1,…,k, the rest only on later tosses, so by independence each term is P(N1=k) qm−1pP(N_1=k)\,q^{m-1}pP(N1​=k)qm−1p, and ∑kP(N1=k)=1\sum_kP(N_1=k)=1∑k​P(N1​=k)=1. Hence P(N2−N1=m)=qm−1pP(N_2-N_1=m)=q^{m-1}pP(N2​−N1​=m)=qm−1p. After the first +1+1+1 the process starts afresh (memorylessness).

    Answer

    N∼N\simN∼Geometric(p)(p)(p), pN(k)=qk−1pp_N(k)=q^{k-1}ppN​(k)=qk−1p, E[N]=1/pE[N]=1/pE[N]=1/p; memoryless; N2−N1∼N_2-N_1\simN2​−N1​∼ Geometric(p)(p)(p) (independent of N1N_1N1​).

    T26-04.4Time to first reach earnings n: E[Tₙ] = n E[T₁] 2026 Tut 4 Q4

    (Gambler of T26-04.3: Xi=±1X_i=\pm1Xi​=±1 with probabilities p,qp,qp,q, Yn=∑i≤nXiY_n=\sum_{i\le n}X_iYn​=∑i≤n​Xi​.) Suppose the gambler keeps tossing the coin indefinitely. Let TnT_nTn​ be the random variable representing the number of tosses required to reach a total earning of nnn (n>0)(n>0)(n>0) for the first time. Find E[Tn]E[T_n]E[Tn​] in terms of E[T1]E[T_1]E[T1​]. (Hint: What can you say about E[Tn]−E[Tn−1]E[T_n]-E[T_{n-1}]E[Tn​]−E[Tn−1​], vs. E[T1]E[T_1]E[T1​]?)

    Solution · written for this guide

    No level can be skipped. Earnings change by ±1\pm1±1 per toss and start at 0, so to reach nnn the walk must first reach n−1n-1n−1: T1<T2<⋯<TnT_1\lt T_2\lt\dots\lt T_nT1​<T2​<⋯<Tn​ and Tn=T1+(T2−T1)+⋯+(Tn−Tn−1).T_n=T_1+(T_2-T_1)+\dots+(T_n-T_{n-1}).Tn​=T1​+(T2​−T1​)+⋯+(Tn​−Tn−1​).

    Each increment is a copy of T1T_1T1​. At time Tk−1T_{k-1}Tk−1​ the earnings are exactly k−1k-1k−1. {Tk−1=t}\{T_{k-1}=t\}{Tk−1​=t} depends only on tosses 1,…,t1,\dots,t1,…,t, and the tosses after ttt are independent of them and have the same law. Reaching kkk from k−1k-1k−1 is the same as reaching +1+1+1 from 0 using the fresh tosses, so Tk−Tk−1T_k-T_{k-1}Tk​−Tk−1​ has the same distribution as T1T_1T1​ (the same "start afresh" argument as for the geometric gap in H26-04.2(d)). In particular E[Tk−Tk−1]=E[T1]E[T_k-T_{k-1}]=E[T_1]E[Tk​−Tk−1​]=E[T1​].

    Linearity of expectation (no independence needed): E[Tn]=∑k=1nE[Tk−Tk−1]=n E[T1](T0=0).E[T_n]=\sum_{k=1}^nE[T_k-T_{k-1}]=n\,E[T_1]\qquad(T_0=0).E[Tn​]=k=1∑n​E[Tk​−Tk−1​]=nE[T1​](T0​=0).

    Answer

    E[Tn]=n E[T1]E[T_n]=n\,E[T_1]E[Tn​]=nE[T1​].

    What is E[T₁]? (beyond the question)

    First-step analysis (topic 5): T1=1T_1=1T1​=1 if the first toss is +1+1+1; otherwise the walk is at −1-1−1 and needs two levels, so E[T1]=1+q⋅2E[T1]E[T_1]=1+q\cdot2E[T_1]E[T1​]=1+q⋅2E[T1​], giving E[T1]=11−2q=12p−1E[T_1]=\frac{1}{1-2q}=\frac{1}{2p-1}E[T1​]=1−2q1​=2p−11​ when p>12p\gt\tfrac12p>21​. For p≤12p\le\tfrac12p≤21​, E[T1]=∞E[T_1]=\inftyE[T1​]=∞ (for p<12p\lt\tfrac12p<21​ the walk may never reach +1+1+1). So E[Tn]=n2p−1E[T_n]=\frac{n}{2p-1}E[Tn​]=2p−1n​ for p>12p\gt\tfrac12p>21​. (Simulated: p=0.7p=0.7p=0.7, n=3n=3n=3 gives ≈7.5\approx7.5≈7.5.)

    PC3.3.8Repeated pass–fail test with halving failure probability PC §3.3 Problem 8

    Suppose you take a pass-fail test repeatedly. Let SkS_kSk​ be the event that you are successful in your kthk^{th}kth try, and FkF_kFk​ the event that you fail in your kthk^{th}kth try. On your first try, you have a 50 percent chance of passing: P(S1)=1−P(F1)=12P(S_1)=1-P(F_1)=\frac{1}{2}P(S1​)=1−P(F1​)=21​. As you take the test more often, your chance of failing goes down: P(Fk)=12P(Fk−1)P(F_k)=\frac{1}{2} P(F_{k-1})P(Fk​)=21​P(Fk−1​), k=2,3,4,…k=2,3,4,\dotsk=2,3,4,… However, the results of different exams are independent. Suppose you take the test repeatedly until you pass for the first time. Let XXX be the total number of tests you take, so Range(X)={1,2,3,… }Range(X)=\{1,2,3,\dots\}Range(X)={1,2,3,…}.

    1. Find P(X=1)P(X=1)P(X=1), P(X=2)P(X=2)P(X=2), P(X=3)P(X=3)P(X=3).
    2. Find a general formula for P(X=k)P(X=k)P(X=k) for k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dotsk=1,2,…
    3. Find the probability that you take the test more than 2 times.
    4. Given that you take the test more than once, find the probability that you take the test exactly twice.
    Solution · written for this guide

    P(Fk)=(12)kP(F_k)=\left(\tfrac12\right)^kP(Fk​)=(21​)k (induction from P(F1)=12P(F_1)=\tfrac12P(F1​)=21​), so P(Sk)=1−2−kP(S_k)=1-2^{-k}P(Sk​)=1−2−k. X=kX=kX=k iff F1∩⋯∩Fk−1∩SkF_1\cap\dots\cap F_{k-1}\cap S_kF1​∩⋯∩Fk−1​∩Sk​; by independence:

    (a)

    P(X=1)=12P(X=1)=\tfrac12P(X=1)=21​; P(X=2)=12⋅34=38P(X=2)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac38P(X=2)=21​⋅43​=83​; P(X=3)=12⋅14⋅78=764P(X=3)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac78=\tfrac{7}{64}P(X=3)=21​⋅41​⋅87​=647​.

    (b)

    P(X=k)=∏j=1k−12−j⋅(1−2−k)=2−k(k−1)2(1−2−k),k≥1.P(X=k)=\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}2^{-j}\cdot\left(1-2^{-k}\right)=2^{-\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\left(1-2^{-k}\right),\quad k\ge1.P(X=k)=j=1∏k−1​2−j⋅(1−2−k)=2−2k(k−1)​(1−2−k),k≥1. (Not geometric: the success probability changes from trial to trial.)

    (c)

    P(X>2)=P(F1∩F2)=12⋅14=18P(X\gt2)=P(F_1\cap F_2)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac18P(X>2)=P(F1​∩F2​)=21​⋅41​=81​ (check: 1−12−381-\tfrac12-\tfrac381−21​−83​).

    (d)

    P(X=2∣X>1)=P(X=2)P(X>1)=3/81/2=34P(X=2\mid X\gt1)=\frac{P(X=2)}{P(X\gt1)}=\frac{3/8}{1/2}=\frac34P(X=2∣X>1)=P(X>1)P(X=2)​=1/23/8​=43​. (Compare memorylessness: a geometric would give P(X=1)=12P(X=1)=\tfrac12P(X=1)=21​ here; this XXX is not memoryless.)

    Answer

    12,38,764\tfrac12,\tfrac38,\tfrac7{64}21​,83​,647​; P(X=k)=2−k(k−1)/2(1−2−k)P(X=k)=2^{-k(k-1)/2}(1-2^{-k})P(X=k)=2−k(k−1)/2(1−2−k); P(X>2)=18P(X\gt2)=\tfrac18P(X>2)=81​; P(X=2∣X>1)=34P(X=2\mid X\gt1)=\tfrac34P(X=2∣X>1)=43​.
